ClusterRole.summary: A ClusterRole is a cluster-level collection of RBAC policy rules. A RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding can use it as one permission set.
ClusterRole.explanation: A ClusterRole stores a set of RBAC policy rules at cluster scope. A RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding can refer to it, and an aggregation rule can let a controller build its rules from other ClusterRoles.

parameters.name: NAME
parameters.description: The ClusterRole name used by the create command.

parameters.name: --verb
parameters.description: Verbs that apply to the resources in the rule.

parameters.name: --resource
parameters.description: Resources and optional API groups targeted by the rule.

parameters.name: --resource-name
parameters.description: Optional names of specific resources to allow.

parameters.name: --non-resource-url
parameters.description: Optional non-resource URL pattern.

parameters.name: --aggregation-rule
parameters.description: Label selector used to aggregate matching ClusterRoles.

ClusterRole.returns: A ClusterRole object is returned by successful create and read operations. List operations return a ClusterRoleList.

example.title: Create and bind a read-only ClusterRole
example.code:
kubectl create clusterrole pod-reader --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods
kubectl create rolebinding pod-reader-binding --clusterrole=pod-reader --serviceaccount=default:app
example.explanation: This creates a ClusterRole that can read Pods, then grants those permissions to a service account in one namespace.

useCases.title: Read selected resources
useCases.scenario: Give an application read access to Pods.

useCases.title: Reuse permissions
useCases.scenario: Grant the same named permission set through several bindings.

useCases.title: Aggregate permissions
useCases.scenario: Build a role from other labeled ClusterRoles.

interview.question: What is a ClusterRole?
interview.answer: A ClusterRole is a cluster-level group of PolicyRules. A RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding can reference it.
interview.followUp: How can one ClusterRole get rules from other ClusterRoles? Use aggregationRule with label selectors; matching roles contribute their permissions.

interview.question: How does a binding use a ClusterRole?
interview.answer: Use a RoleBinding when access should be granted in one namespace. The binding can still reference a ClusterRole.
interview.followUp: When should ClusterRoleBinding be used? Use it when the grant itself should apply across the cluster.

interview.question: How do you create a ClusterRole?
interview.answer: Create one with kubectl create clusterrole NAME, then provide verbs and resources, such as --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods. You can also specify an API group, subresource, resource names, or a non-resource URL.
interview.followUp: How can you preview creation without saving it? Use --dry-run=client to print the object, or --dry-run=server to submit it without persisting it.

keyPoints: It groups RBAC permissions into one named object at cluster scope.
Bindings refer to the ClusterRole as one permission set instead of copying each rule.
The rules field contains the permissions granted by the role.
An optional aggregation rule selects other ClusterRoles whose rules should be combined.
The kubectl command can create a read-only Pod role with get, list, and watch verbs.
gotchas: Do not edit rules directly when aggregationRule is set. The controller manages them and can replace direct changes.
A matching label on any selected ClusterRole adds that role's permissions to the aggregated role.

ClusterRoleBinding.summary: A ClusterRoleBinding gives users, groups, or service accounts the permissions defined by a ClusterRole. It applies the referenced role at cluster scope.
ClusterRoleBinding.explanation: A ClusterRoleBinding connects a ClusterRole with the users, groups, or service accounts that receive its permissions. The referenced ClusterRole is global, so the binding grants its rules across the cluster.

parameters.name: NAME
parameters.description: Binding name used in the resource URL and metadata.

parameters.name: --clusterrole
parameters.description: The ClusterRole referenced by roleRef.

parameters.name: --user
parameters.description: Users that receive the ClusterRole permissions; repeat the flag for multiple users.

parameters.name: --group
parameters.description: Groups that receive the ClusterRole permissions; repeat the flag for multiple groups.

parameters.name: --serviceaccount
parameters.description: Service accounts in namespace:name form.

ClusterRoleBinding.returns: The Kubernetes API returns a ClusterRoleBinding for successful create, read, update, and patch operations. Delete operations return Status.

example.title: Bind a ServiceAccount to a ClusterRole
example.code:
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: read-nodes
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: app
  namespace: default
roleRef:
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: node-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
example.explanation: This binds the node-reader ClusterRole to the app ServiceAccount in the default namespace.

useCases.title: Grant cluster-wide access to a service account
useCases.scenario: A controller or driver needs selected permissions across cluster resources.

useCases.title: Bind a role to users or groups
useCases.scenario: Several teams or people need the same ClusterRole permissions.

useCases.title: Manage access with YAML
useCases.scenario: An administrator wants to define the binding declaratively.

interview.question: What does a ClusterRoleBinding do?
interview.answer: A ClusterRoleBinding grants the permissions in one ClusterRole to its listed subjects. Because it is cluster-scoped, those permissions apply across the cluster.
interview.followUp: Can it reference a Role? No. Its roleRef is limited to a ClusterRole in the global namespace.

interview.question: What is stored in subjects?
interview.answer: The subjects field identifies the recipients of the permissions. A subject can be a user, group, or service account; service accounts include their namespace.
interview.followUp: How would you bind several recipients? Add multiple entries to subjects, or use repeated kubectl flags for users and groups.

interview.question: How can you create a ClusterRoleBinding from kubectl?
interview.answer: Use kubectl create clusterrolebinding NAME with --clusterrole and one or more subject flags, such as --user, --group, or --serviceaccount. The command creates a binding for the selected ClusterRole.
interview.followUp: How can you test the request without saving it? Use --dry-run=client to print the object, or --dry-run=server to send it without persistence.

keyPoints: The binding points to an existing ClusterRole; it does not copy or define that role's rules.
Use subjects to list the identities that receive the ClusterRole permissions.
The kubectl create clusterrolebinding command creates a binding for one selected ClusterRole.
The group option can be repeated when several groups need the same binding.
Specify a service account with its namespace and name in the serviceaccount option.
gotchas: The roleRef must point to a ClusterRole, not a namespaced Role.
You cannot change roleRef after creation; create a new binding if the referenced role must change.
The referenced ClusterRole must exist and be resolvable for authorization to work.

ConfigMap.summary: A ConfigMap stores non-confidential configuration as key-value pairs. Pods can use it as environment variables, command arguments, files in a volume, or data read through the Kubernetes API.
ConfigMap.explanation: A ConfigMap stores non-confidential configuration as key-value pairs. A Pod can use the values as environment variables, command arguments, or files in a volume. The ConfigMap and Pod must be in the same namespace when the Pod refers to it directly.
ConfigMap.syntax:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: <name>
data:
  <key>: <value>
# Optional:
# binaryData:
# immutable: true

parameters.name: apiVersion
parameters.description: API version for the object.

parameters.name: kind
parameters.description: Object type. Use ConfigMap.

parameters.name: metadata
parameters.description: Object identity, including its name and namespace.

parameters.name: data
parameters.description: Text configuration values keyed by valid names.

parameters.name: binaryData
parameters.description: Base64-encoded binary values keyed by valid names.

parameters.name: immutable
parameters.description: When true, data and binaryData cannot be changed.

example.title: Use a ConfigMap key in a Pod
example.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-settings
data:
  DATABASE_HOST: localhost
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: configmap-demo
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: busybox:latest
      command: ["sh", "-c", "echo $DATABASE_HOST; sleep 3600"]
      env:
        - name: DATABASE_HOST
          valueFrom:
            configMapKeyRef:
              name: app-settings
              key: DATABASE_HOST
example.explanation: This creates a ConfigMap and uses one of its keys as a Pod environment variable.

useCases.title: Separate deployment settings from code
useCases.scenario: An application needs different database hosts in local and cloud environments.

useCases.title: Share configuration through a volume
useCases.scenario: Several Pods need the same read-only configuration files.

useCases.title: Read updates through the Kubernetes API
useCases.scenario: An application must observe configuration changes and react to them.

related: Configure a Pod to Use a ConfigMap

interview.question: What is a ConfigMap, and how can a Pod use it?
interview.answer: A ConfigMap stores non-confidential configuration in key-value pairs. A Pod can consume it through environment variables, command arguments, a read-only volume, or the Kubernetes API.
interview.followUp: How can an application react to changes?

interview.question: What happens when a mounted ConfigMap changes?
interview.answer: A volume-mounted ConfigMap is eventually refreshed by the kubelet after the object changes. The delay depends on the kubelet sync period and its cache propagation method.
interview.followUp: What happens with an environment-variable reference?

interview.question: How do you make a ConfigMap immutable?
interview.answer: Set immutable to true. Kubernetes then prevents changes to data and binaryData; only metadata can change. To change the contents, delete and recreate the ConfigMap.
interview.followUp: Why might this help cluster performance?

keyPoints: It stores configuration separately from application code.
A Pod has several built-in ways to read ConfigMap values.
Use data for text values.
Use binaryData for bytes that are not valid UTF-8 text.
Direct Pod references require the objects to share a namespace.
The immutable field was introduced in Kubernetes v1.19.
Immutable ConfigMaps are a stable feature in Kubernetes v1.21 and later.
gotchas: Do not store confidential data in a ConfigMap. Use a Secret instead.
A ConfigMap is not suitable for large data. Use a volume or another storage service for larger settings.
Restart the Pod after changing a ConfigMap used through environment variables.
Do not use a subPath mount when the container must receive later ConfigMap changes.

Control plane.sourceTitle: Communication between Nodes and the Control Plane | Kubernetes
Control plane.summary: Kubernetes uses the API server as the central communication point between nodes, Pods, and the control plane. Konnectivity provides a TCP proxy for control-plane traffic to nodes when direct network access is not suitable.
Control plane.explanation: The control plane manages nodes and Pods. The API server is the central entry point: nodes, Pods, and control plane components use it for API requests. The scheduler chooses nodes for new Pods, controllers react to cluster changes, and etcd stores cluster data.

example.title: Inspect cluster resources
example.code:
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get pods --all-namespaces
example.explanation: These commands show the worker nodes and Pods managed by the cluster control plane.

useCases.title: Use Konnectivity as a TCP proxy
useCases.scenario: Protect control-plane-to-node traffic across separate networks.

useCases.title: Use a cluster root certificate and client credentials
useCases.scenario: Let a kubelet authenticate to the API server.

useCases.title: Separate control-plane and worker-node roles
useCases.scenario: Understand cluster responsibilities.

interview.question: How do nodes communicate with the control plane?
interview.answer: Kubernetes uses a hub-and-spoke API pattern. Requests from nodes and their Pods go to the API server, while other control plane components are not designed to expose remote services.
interview.followUp: How can control-plane-to-node traffic cross a network boundary? Use Konnectivity, which proxies TCP traffic through agent connections initiated from the nodes network.

interview.question: How does a node authenticate securely to the API server?
interview.answer: The API server accepts secure HTTPS connections. Nodes need the cluster root certificate and valid client credentials; kubelet credentials can use a client certificate.
interview.followUp: How can kubelet certificates be provisioned automatically? Use TLS bootstrapping to provision kubelet client certificates.

interview.question: What do the scheduler and controllers do?
interview.answer: The scheduler watches for new Pods without an assigned node and selects a node using resources, constraints, affinity, locality, interference, and deadlines. Controllers then respond to changes such as failed nodes or unsatisfied replicas.
interview.followUp: How does Kubernetes connect cloud-specific behavior? The cloud-controller-manager uses plugins and controllers for cloud integration, including node, route, and service behavior.

keyPoints: The API server is the single API destination for nodes and the Pods running on them.
The control plane coordinates the cluster, while worker nodes host application Pods.
etcd stores Kubernetes cluster data and should have a backup plan.
The scheduler assigns newly created, unassigned Pods to suitable nodes.
The controller manager combines several logically separate controllers into one process.
Konnectivity uses a server in the control-plane network and agents in the nodes network.
gotchas: Do not choose SSH tunnels for new designs unless you have a specific reason. Konnectivity replaces this communication method.
Node-to-service, node-to-Pod, and node-to-node connections that lack certificate validation and client credentials should not cross an untrusted network.

CronJob.summary: A CronJob creates Kubernetes Jobs on a repeating schedule. Use it for recurring tasks such as backups or reports.
CronJob.explanation: A CronJob is a Kubernetes resource that creates Jobs on a repeating schedule. The Job template defines the Pods and command to run; the controller checks the schedule and starts new Jobs when due.
CronJob.syntax:
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: <name>
spec:
  schedule: <cron-expression>
  jobTemplate: <JobSpec>

parameters.name: spec.schedule
parameters.description: Cron expression or supported macro that controls when Jobs are created.

parameters.name: spec.jobTemplate
parameters.description: Template for the Jobs created by the CronJob.

parameters.name: spec.concurrencyPolicy
parameters.description: How to handle overlapping Jobs: Allow, Forbid, or Replace.

parameters.name: spec.startingDeadlineSeconds
parameters.description: Maximum delay, in seconds, allowed for a missed start.

parameters.name: spec.suspend
parameters.description: Pauses future executions when true.

parameters.name: spec.successfulJobsHistoryLimit
parameters.description: Number of successful finished Jobs to retain.

parameters.name: spec.failedJobsHistoryLimit
parameters.description: Number of failed finished Jobs to retain.

parameters.name: spec.timeZone
parameters.description: Time-zone database name used to interpret the schedule.

CronJob.returns: A CronJob resource and, at scheduled times, Job objects that manage Pods.

example.title: Run a command every five minutes
example.code:
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: hello
spec:
  schedule: "*/5 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
            - name: hello
              image: busybox:1.36
              command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "date; echo Hello"]
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
example.explanation: This creates a CronJob that starts a Job every five minutes. The Job runs a BusyBox command in a Pod.

useCases.title: Backups
useCases.scenario: Run a database backup at regular times.

useCases.title: Reports and exports
useCases.scenario: Create a periodic report or data export.

useCases.title: Scheduled maintenance
useCases.scenario: Run maintenance work on a recurring schedule.

interview.question: What is a CronJob, and what does it create?
interview.answer: A CronJob creates Kubernetes Job objects according to its schedule. Each Job then manages the Pods that perform the task.
interview.followUp: What happens if the controller misses many schedules? If more than 100 schedules are missed, it does not start the Job and logs an error.

interview.question: How does concurrencyPolicy work?
interview.answer: Allow permits concurrent Jobs and is the default. Forbid skips a run while the previous Job is active. Replace cancels the active Job and starts a new one.
interview.followUp: Does this policy coordinate different CronJobs? No. It only applies to Jobs created by the same CronJob.

interview.question: What belongs in jobTemplate, and what happens after an update?
interview.answer: The jobTemplate is required and has the same schema as a Job, except it is nested and has no apiVersion or kind. Edits affect only new Jobs; existing Jobs and Pods continue unchanged.
interview.followUp: How can old completed Jobs be limited? Set successfulJobsHistoryLimit and failedJobsHistoryLimit; their defaults are 3 and 1.

keyPoints: Use a CronJob for repeated work such as backups or report generation.
The required jobTemplate describes each Job, including its Pod template and command.
startingDeadlineSeconds limits how late a missed Job may start; after the limit, that run is skipped.
concurrencyPolicy controls overlap: Allow, Forbid, or Replace.
Set spec.suspend to true to pause future executions while leaving already-started Jobs alone.
successfulJobsHistoryLimit keeps three successful completed Jobs by default.
failedJobsHistoryLimit keeps one failed completed Job by default.
Use spec.timeZone with a valid time-zone name when the schedule must use a specific zone.
gotchas: Scheduling is approximate. In some situations, Kubernetes can create two Jobs or create none, so the Job should be idempotent.
A deadline below 10 seconds can prevent scheduling because the controller checks CronJobs every 10 seconds.
Do not put CRON_TZ or TZ in the schedule. Use the separate timeZone field instead.

CustomResourceDefinition.summary: A CustomResourceDefinition (CRD) adds a new resource type to the Kubernetes API. Kubernetes serves and stores objects of that type, and a custom controller can reconcile them into a declarative API.
CustomResourceDefinition.explanation: A CustomResourceDefinition adds a new resource type to the Kubernetes API. It defines the group, versions, names, scope, and validation schema. Kubernetes then serves the resource and stores its objects. A custom controller can watch those objects and make the cluster match their declared desired state.
CustomResourceDefinition.syntax:
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
spec:
  group: <group>
  scope: Namespaced | Cluster
  names: { plural, singular, kind }
  versions: [{ name, served, storage, schema }]

parameters.name: spec.group
parameters.description: The API group for the custom resource.

parameters.name: spec.versions
parameters.description: The versions that Kubernetes serves and stores.

parameters.name: spec.scope
parameters.description: Whether objects are namespaced or cluster-scoped.

parameters.name: spec.names
parameters.description: The plural, singular, kind, and optional short names.

parameters.name: spec.versions[].schema.openAPIV3Schema
parameters.description: The OpenAPI v3 schema for custom object fields.

CustomResourceDefinition.returns: A new Kubernetes API resource and endpoint for storing and managing custom objects.

example.title: Create a CRD and custom object
example.code:
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: crontabs.stable.example.com
spec:
  group: stable.example.com
  scope: Namespaced
  names:
    plural: crontabs
    singular: crontab
    kind: CronTab
    shortNames:
      - ct
  versions:
    - name: v1
      served: true
      storage: true
      schema:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            spec:
              type: object
              properties:
                image:
                  type: string
---
apiVersion: stable.example.com/v1
kind: CronTab
metadata:
  name: example
spec:
  image: example:1
example.explanation: Create the CRD first, then create an object that uses its group, version, and kind.

useCases.title: Add a simple custom API resource
useCases.scenario: An application needs a small, structured API object that users can manage with Kubernetes tools.

useCases.title: Build a declarative controller API
useCases.scenario: A team needs Kubernetes to store desired state while a controller performs reconciliation.

useCases.title: Enable field-based selection
useCases.scenario: Clients need to filter custom objects by selected spec fields.

interview.question: What does a CRD provide?
interview.answer: A CRD declaratively defines a new API resource. Kubernetes creates the REST endpoint, validates objects with the schema, and stores the objects; no custom API server is required.
interview.followUp: When would an aggregated API be better? It is better when the resource needs specialized behavior or more flexible API-server logic.

interview.question: How does resource scope work?
interview.answer: The CRD sets `spec.scope` to either `Namespaced` or `Cluster`. A namespaced resource is tied to a namespace, while a cluster-scoped resource is not.
interview.followUp: What happens to namespaced custom objects when their namespace is deleted? Kubernetes deletes those objects with the namespace.

interview.question: How are custom objects validated?
interview.answer: The schema uses OpenAPI v3.0 rules to validate custom fields during creation and updates. It can enforce types and constraints such as patterns, minimums, and maximums.
interview.followUp: What happens to an undeclared field? The API server usually prunes it before persistence unless unknown fields are explicitly preserved.

keyPoints: A CRD declares the resource name and the schema for its objects.
Kubernetes provides the API endpoint and persistence for CRD objects.
Choose whether the custom resource belongs to namespaces or the whole cluster.
After installation, use kubectl to create, list, and inspect custom objects.
A controller can act on the declared object state and reconcile the cluster.
Declare extra fields that clients can use with field selectors.
gotchas: Deleting a CRD also deletes every custom object stored under that resource.
A v1 CRD must have a structural OpenAPI schema.
Unknown fields are normally removed before the object is stored.

DaemonSet.summary: A DaemonSet keeps a copy of a Pod on every eligible node. It adds Pods when matching nodes appear and removes them when nodes no longer qualify.
DaemonSet.explanation: A DaemonSet keeps a copy of a Pod on every eligible node. The controller adds Pods when matching nodes appear and removes them when nodes no longer qualify.
DaemonSet.syntax:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: <name>
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels: <labels>
  template: <pod-template>

parameters.name: apiVersion
parameters.description: Identifies the DaemonSet API group and version.

parameters.name: kind
parameters.description: Must be DaemonSet.

parameters.name: metadata
parameters.description: Object metadata, including a valid DNS subdomain name.

parameters.name: spec
parameters.description: Desired state, including selector and Pod template.

DaemonSet.returns: A DaemonSet resource that manages Pods on eligible nodes.

example.title: Basic DaemonSet
example.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: node-logger
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: node-logger
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: node-logger
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: logger
        image: busybox:1.37
        command: ["sh", "-c", "while true; do date; sleep 30; done"]
example.explanation: This creates one continuously running Pod on each eligible node.

useCases.title: Node log collection
useCases.scenario: A cluster needs a log collector on each node.

useCases.title: Node-level services
useCases.scenario: Every node needs a networking helper or storage agent.

useCases.title: Node monitoring
useCases.scenario: A node monitoring process must run across selected hardware.

useCases.title: Hardware-specific agents
useCases.scenario: Different hardware groups need different resources or flags.

interview.question: What problem does a DaemonSet solve?
interview.answer: A DaemonSet ensures that one copy of a Pod runs on every eligible node. It adds Pods for new matching nodes and removes them when nodes stop matching.
interview.followUp: How can eligibility be limited? Use nodeSelector or node affinity in the Pod template; the controller then creates Pods only on matching nodes.

interview.question: How do DaemonSet update strategies differ?
interview.answer: The default is RollingUpdate. It replaces old Pods automatically in a controlled way; OnDelete waits until an operator deletes old Pods.
interview.followUp: What setting limits disruption? Set rollingUpdate.maxUnavailable, and optionally use minReadySeconds and maxSurge.

interview.question: Why must the selector match the Pod template labels?
interview.answer: The selector identifies the Pods managed by the DaemonSet and must match the template labels. It is immutable after creation to prevent accidental orphaning.
interview.followUp: What happens if the selector and template labels differ? The API rejects the configuration.

keyPoints: Use a DaemonSet when node-level work needs one Pod on every node or on a selected set of nodes.
New eligible nodes receive a Pod automatically.
Pods belonging to removed nodes are cleaned up automatically.
The template defines the Pod that the DaemonSet creates.
The template must use RestartPolicy Always, or omit it so Kubernetes applies that default.
Add tolerations in the template when the DaemonSet must run on tainted nodes beyond the controller's automatic tolerations.
gotchas: The selector must match the labels in the Pod template. After creation, the selector cannot be changed.
Deleting with orphan cascading leaves the existing Pods behind.

Deployment.summary: A Deployment declares how an application’s Pods should run. Kubernetes uses ReplicaSets to create, update, scale, and replace those Pods.
Deployment.explanation: A Deployment stores the desired state for an application. Its controller creates and manages ReplicaSets, which create Pods and replace them during updates. By default, updates use a rolling strategy that limits unavailable and extra Pods.
Deployment.syntax:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: <name>
spec:
  replicas: <number>
  selector:
    matchLabels: <labels>
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: <matching-labels>
    spec:
      containers: <container-list>

parameters.name: spec.replicas
parameters.description: Desired number of Pods. Defaults to 1.

parameters.name: spec.selector
parameters.description: Selector for Pods managed by the Deployment; it must match the template labels.

parameters.name: spec.template
parameters.description: Template for Pods created by the Deployment.

parameters.name: spec.strategy
parameters.description: Update method: Recreate or RollingUpdate. Defaults to RollingUpdate.

Deployment.returns: A Deployment object with desired configuration and observed status, including replica counts, conditions, and update progress.

example.title: Create three nginx Pods
example.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nginx-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.25
example.explanation: This creates three nginx Pods through a ReplicaSet.

useCases.title: Create a workload
useCases.scenario: Start an application with a chosen number of identical Pods.

useCases.title: Roll out an update
useCases.scenario: Change a container image while replacing Pods gradually.

useCases.title: Roll back
useCases.scenario: Return to a previous revision after an unstable release.

useCases.title: Pause a rollout
useCases.scenario: Temporarily stop rollout processing while making several template edits.

interview.question: What does a Deployment manage?
interview.answer: A Deployment describes the desired Pod state. The Deployment controller creates ReplicaSets, and those ReplicaSets create the Pods. The controller then changes the actual state toward the desired state.
interview.followUp: What happens if a node hosting a Pod fails? The controller replaces the failed instance so the Deployment can continue to provide the requested replicas.

interview.question: How does a Deployment update Pods?
interview.answer: A Pod-template change creates a new ReplicaSet. Kubernetes gradually increases the new ReplicaSet and decreases the old one. The default RollingUpdate settings allow 25% extra Pods and 25% unavailable Pods.
interview.followUp: How would you prevent too many unavailable Pods? Set strategy.rollingUpdate.maxUnavailable to a suitable number or percentage, while ensuring maxSurge is compatible.

interview.question: What is the purpose of spec.selector?
interview.answer: The selector identifies the Pods managed by the Deployment. It must match the Pod template labels. All selector requirements must be satisfied.
interview.followUp: Why avoid overlapping selectors? Two controllers could target the same Pods and interfere with each other.

keyPoints: A Deployment is suited to applications that usually do not keep local state.
The controller continually moves the cluster toward the state declared in the Deployment.
Kubernetes records a new revision when a new ReplicaSet is created for an update.
You can roll back when the current release is not stable.
Pausing lets you make several template changes before starting one rollout.
spec.replicas sets how many Pod copies the Deployment should maintain.
gotchas: Let the Deployment controller manage its ReplicaSets. Do not edit those ReplicaSets directly.
Changing the Pod template starts a rollout. Changing only the replica count does not.
The selector must match the labels in the Pod template and must not overlap with another controller.
Do not edit the automatically added pod-template-hash label.

etcd.summary: Operate etcd as a protected, multi-member store for Kubernetes cluster data. Use TLS, replace failed members promptly, and back up snapshots regularly so the cluster can be recovered.
etcd.explanation: etcd stores Kubernetes cluster data. Run it with multiple members for high availability, protect access with TLS, and make regular encrypted backups. Use etcdctl for network operations and etcdutl for local data files, snapshots, and recovery.
etcd.syntax:
etcdctl --endpoints=<endpoint> snapshot save <backup-file>
etcdutl --write-out=table snapshot status <snapshot-file>

example.title: Back up and check an etcd snapshot
example.code:
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/peer.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/peer.key \
  snapshot save snapshot.db

etcdutl --write-out=table snapshot status snapshot.db
example.explanation: This creates an etcd snapshot and then checks its status with etcdutl.

useCases.title: Run a highly available etcd cluster
useCases.scenario: A production Kubernetes cluster needs a durable backing store.

useCases.title: Back up cluster state
useCases.scenario: A control plane may be lost or corrupted.

useCases.title: Replace a failed member
useCases.scenario: One etcd member stops working.

useCases.title: Restrict and encrypt access
useCases.scenario: Only the Kubernetes API server should reach etcd.

interview.question: What is etcd used for in Kubernetes?
interview.answer: etcd is Kubernetes' consistent, highly available key-value store for cluster data. A production setup should use multiple members, and the documentation recommends five members for production.
interview.followUp: Why use an odd number of members? It supports quorum while limiting unnecessary members; the page specifically says to run etcd with an odd number of members.

interview.question: What is the difference between etcdctl and etcdutl?
interview.answer: Use etcdctl for operations over the network, such as checking health, managing members, and saving snapshots. Use etcdutl for operations on data files, including snapshot checks, restoration, and defragmentation.
interview.followUp: Which tool should verify a snapshot? Use etcdutl; the page says the etcdctl snapshot-status command is deprecated.

interview.question: How should an etcd cluster be restored?
interview.answer: First stop all API servers. Restore the state on every etcd member, then restart the API servers; restarting the scheduler, controller manager, and kubelets is also recommended to avoid stale data.
interview.followUp: What should happen if a member fails? Remove the failed member, add a replacement, start it with the existing cluster state, and update API-server endpoints if needed.

keyPoints: Kubernetes uses etcd as the backing store for all cluster data.
Use an odd number of members, such as three or five.
The production recommendation is a static five-member cluster.
Treat etcd access like root access and allow it only to required nodes.
Use etcdctl for network-based client and administration commands.
Use multiple members in production and make regular backups.
gotchas: A single-member cluster is not suitable for production.
Adding members does not increase etcd performance or capacity.
Stop every API server before restoring etcd, then restart the API servers afterward.
Protect snapshot files because they contain sensitive cluster data.

Gateway.summary: Gateway API is a set of Kubernetes resources for creating network infrastructure and routing traffic. GatewayClass selects the controller, Gateway defines the endpoint, and route resources send matching requests to backends.
Gateway.explanation: Gateway API uses related resources to describe network infrastructure and route traffic. A GatewayClass identifies the controller, a Gateway defines the traffic endpoint, and an HTTPRoute or GRPCRoute sends matching requests to backend endpoints such as a Service.

example.title: Gateway with an HTTP route
example.code:
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: example-gateway
spec:
  gatewayClassName: example-class
  listeners:
  - name: http
    protocol: HTTP
    port: 80
    hostname: www.example.com
    allowedRoutes:
      namespaces:
        from: Same
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: example-httproute
spec:
  parentRefs:
  - name: example-gateway
  hostnames:
  - www.example.com
  rules:
  - matches:
    - path:
        type: PathPrefix
        value: /login
    backendRefs:
    - name: example-svc
      port: 8080
example.explanation: This creates an HTTP Gateway and sends matching requests to a Service.

useCases.title: HTTP traffic routing
useCases.scenario: Expose an HTTP application through a cloud load balancer or in-cluster proxy.

useCases.title: gRPC traffic routing
useCases.scenario: Send gRPC requests to Services using host or method-based routing.

useCases.title: Role-based ownership
useCases.scenario: Let infrastructure, cluster, and application teams manage different parts of service networking.

interview.question: What is the relationship between GatewayClass and Gateway?
interview.answer: GatewayClass describes a group of Gateways managed by one controller. A Gateway must refer to a GatewayClass, whose controllerName identifies that controller.
interview.followUp: What does a Gateway listener control? It defines protocol, port, hostname, and which routes can attach to that listener.

interview.question: What does HTTPRoute do?
interview.answer: HTTPRoute defines HTTP request matching and forwarding rules from a Gateway listener to backend network endpoints. It can match hostnames and paths and reference a Service backend.
interview.followUp: How would you restrict route attachment? Configure allowedRoutes on the relevant Gateway listener, including its namespace policy.

interview.question: Describe the request flow through a Gateway.
interview.answer: A client resolves the Gateway hostname to one or more Gateway addresses, sends the request there, and the proxy matches the Host header and route rules. The proxy can apply filters and then forward the request to backends.
interview.followUp: What happens when a route uses a path match? The implementation can use that match, together with other route criteria, to select the backend rule.

keyPoints: Gateway API provides Kubernetes resources for creating network infrastructure and routing service traffic.
Its resources separate responsibilities between infrastructure providers, cluster operators, and application developers.
GatewayClass groups Gateways that share configuration and identifies the controller that manages them.
Gateway represents a traffic endpoint, such as a cloud load balancer or an in-cluster proxy.
HTTPRoute maps HTTP requests received by a Gateway listener to backend endpoints.
GRPCRoute applies routing rules to gRPC requests and forwards them to backend endpoints.
gotchas: Routes in another namespace need an appropriate allowedRoutes setting on the Gateway listener.
The API kinds are Custom Resources, so install the Gateway API CRDs and a compatible implementation before using them.
Migrating from Ingress requires a one-time conversion to Gateway API resources.

Helm chart.summary: The helmCharts field lets Kustomize fetch or load Helm charts and render their templates. Run kustomize build with --enable-helm to use this generator.
Helm chart.explanation: Kustomize uses each helmCharts entry to fetch or load a Helm chart and render its templates. Remote charts use repo; without repo, Kustomize looks in chartHome. The generator is disabled unless the build command includes --enable-helm.
Helm chart.syntax:
helmCharts:
  - name: <chart>
    repo: <repository-url>
    version: <version>
    releaseName: <release-name>
    namespace: <namespace>

kustomize build --enable-helm <directory>

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Chart name.

parameters.name: repo
parameters.description: Optional chart repository URL.

parameters.name: version
parameters.description: Optional chart version.

parameters.name: releaseName
parameters.description: Optional Helm release name.

parameters.name: namespace
parameters.description: Optional namespace passed to Helm.

parameters.name: valuesFile
parameters.description: Optional values file path.

parameters.name: valuesInline
parameters.description: Inline value mappings.

parameters.name: valuesMerge
parameters.description: How inline values are combined: merge, override, or replace.

parameters.name: includeCRDs
parameters.description: Whether to generate CustomResourceDefinitions.

parameters.name: skipHooks
parameters.description: Whether to skip hooks.

parameters.name: additionalValuesFiles
parameters.description: Local value file paths added to the current values file.

parameters.name: skipTests
parameters.description: Whether to skip tests in the output.

example.title: Render a Helm chart with Kustomize
example.code:
helmCharts:
  - name: nginx
    repo: https://example.com/charts
    version: 1.2.3
    releaseName: web
    namespace: default
    includeCRDs: true

# Run:
# kustomize build --enable-helm .
example.explanation: This configuration renders the nginx chart with Kustomize. The command enables the Helm chart inflation generator.

useCases.title: Render a chart inside Kustomize
useCases.scenario: A project already uses Helm charts but needs Kustomize to combine the rendered resources with other manifest transformations.

useCases.title: Select chart and release settings
useCases.scenario: A chart requires a specific chart release and Kubernetes namespace during template rendering.

useCases.title: Control generated resources
useCases.scenario: A chart includes CRDs or tests that should be controlled in generated output.

interview.question: How do you enable Helm chart rendering in Kustomize?
interview.answer: Add one or more objects under helmCharts in kustomization.yaml. Then run kustomize build --enable-helm so Kustomize can fetch or load and render the chart.
interview.followUp: What happens without repo? Kustomize tries to load the chart locally from chartHome.

interview.question: Which fields select and configure a chart?
interview.answer: Use repo for a remote chart and version to select its version. If version is omitted, the latest chart version is used.
interview.followUp: Which fields control rendered release metadata? releaseName sets the release name, and namespace supplies Helm's --namespace value.

interview.question: How can chart values be supplied?
interview.answer: valuesInline places values directly in the kustomization, while valuesMerge controls how they combine with the chart values. Its allowed modes are merge, override, and replace; override is the default.
interview.followUp: How can you add more value files? Set additionalValuesFiles to a list of local paths.

keyPoints: Each helmCharts item causes Kustomize to obtain and render one Helm chart.
name identifies the chart.
repo points to the chart repository; it is optional.
version is optional, and the latest version is selected when it is absent.
Set includeCRDs to true when the rendered output should include CustomResourceDefinitions.
skipHooks prevents hooks from running during chart inflation.
skipTests removes chart tests from the generated output.
gotchas: The generator does not run unless you add --enable-helm to the kustomize build command.
This built-in supports only a limited subset of Helm features.
Default output can differ from helm install because Kustomize renders all templates unless hooks are skipped.

helm install.sourceTitle: Creating a PostgreSQL Cluster using Helm
helm install.summary: This example uses Helm to deploy a PostgreSQL master and an asynchronous read-only replica on Kubernetes. It also shows how to test replication and scale replicas.
helm install.explanation: Helm installs a chart that creates a PostgreSQL master, a read-only replica, and services for both. The replica uses streaming replication and can be scaled by changing the replication controller count.

example.title: Install and check a PostgreSQL chart
example.code:
helm install ./crunchy-postgres
kubectl get services
psql -h crunchy-master -U postgres postgres -c 'table pg_stat_replication'
example.explanation: This installs the chart, lists its services, and checks whether the master has a replication connection.

useCases.title: Database deployment
useCases.scenario: Deploy a simple PostgreSQL master and replica in Kubernetes.

useCases.title: Replication testing
useCases.scenario: Check whether the replica is receiving changes from the master.

useCases.title: Read scaling
useCases.scenario: Add more read-only database endpoints for query traffic.

interview.question: What resources does this example create?
interview.answer: The chart creates a master service, a replica service, a PostgreSQL 9.5 master pod, and a replication controller for the replica. The master accepts writes, while the replica is read-only.
interview.followUp: How can read capacity be increased? Scale the replica replication controller, for example with kubectl scale rc crunchy-replica --replicas=2.

interview.question: How do you verify replication?
interview.answer: Run the pg_stat_replication query through the master service. A returned row shows that the master is replicating to the replica.
interview.followUp: How can the replicated data be checked? Create data through crunchy-master, then query the same table through crunchy-replica.

interview.question: How do you add read-only replicas?
interview.answer: Install the chart with Helm, then scale the replica replication controller with kubectl. The controller lets the number of read-only replicas be changed on demand.
interview.followUp: What delay should be expected after scaling? A new replica can take about 60 seconds to start and begin replicating.

keyPoints: The example creates separate master and replica services, plus database workloads for PostgreSQL 9.5.
The master database runs in a pod and handles read-write database traffic.
The replica is managed by a replication controller, which supports changing its replica count.
The replica workload is described by the replica replication-controller template.
The replica service provides a stable endpoint for connecting to replica containers.
Use kubectl scale to increase the number of read-only replicas.
gotchas: The replica may not be ready immediately. Wait about one minute before checking replication.
After scaling, a new replica also needs about 60 seconds before it starts replicating.

helm upgrade.sourceTitle: Deploy and Access the Kubernetes Dashboard
helm upgrade.summary: Kubernetes Dashboard is a web UI for viewing and managing cluster resources and applications. The official page says it is deprecated and unmaintained, and recommends Headlamp for new installations.
helm upgrade.explanation: The command installs a Helm release named kubernetes-dashboard from the kubernetes-dashboard chart. It creates the kubernetes-dashboard namespace if needed and places the release there. The same command also updates an existing release.

example.title: Install or update the Dashboard
example.code:
helm repo add kubernetes-dashboard https://kubernetes.github.io/dashboard/
helm upgrade --install kubernetes-dashboard kubernetes-dashboard/kubernetes-dashboard \
  --create-namespace --namespace kubernetes-dashboard
example.explanation: This adds the Dashboard chart repository and installs or updates the release in its own namespace.

useCases.title: Inspect cluster resources
useCases.scenario: A learner needs a browser view of applications and cluster resources.

useCases.title: Deploy an application
useCases.scenario: An operator wants to create a Deployment and optional Service through a wizard.

useCases.title: Use local port forwarding
useCases.scenario: A developer needs to open the UI from a local workstation.

interview.question: How do you install Kubernetes Dashboard?
interview.answer: Use helm repo add to register the official chart repository. Then run helm upgrade --install with the release name, chart name, namespace, and --create-namespace.
interview.followUp: What does --create-namespace do? It creates the target namespace when it does not already exist.

interview.question: How can you access the Dashboard locally?
interview.answer: Run kubectl -n kubernetes-dashboard port-forward svc/kubernetes-dashboard-kong-proxy 8443:443. Then open https://localhost:8443 on the same machine.
interview.followUp: Can another machine use that forwarded address? No. The page says the UI is available only from the machine running port-forward.

interview.question: What authentication and permission details must an operator know?
interview.answer: Dashboard uses minimal RBAC permissions by default. Access requires a bearer token, and the sample user in the tutorial has administrative privileges.
interview.followUp: Why should the sample user not be used in production? Its administrative permissions grant broad control over the cluster.

keyPoints: Dashboard provides a web interface for working with Kubernetes resources and applications.
A cluster does not include Dashboard automatically. Install it separately when needed.
The deployment wizard can create an application as a Deployment and can also create a Service.
The wizard accepts either manually entered details or a YAML or JSON manifest file.
gotchas: Do not choose Dashboard for a new installation without reviewing its maintenance status. The official page recommends Headlamp instead.
Use a bearer token to sign in. Other login methods are not supported by Dashboard.
The tutorial's sample user is highly privileged and should be used only for learning, not as a production account.

HorizontalPodAutoscaler.summary: HorizontalPodAutoscaler automatically changes a scalable workload's Pod count to match demand. It can scale from resource, custom, object, or external metrics.
HorizontalPodAutoscaler.explanation: The HPA controller reads metrics for Pods selected by the target workload, compares their current values with configured targets, and changes the workload's replica count. It can use resource, custom, object, or external metrics. With several metrics, it chooses the largest desired replica count. Scale-down recommendations are stabilized to reduce rapid fluctuations.
HorizontalPodAutoscaler.syntax:
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: ...
  minReplicas: ...
  maxReplicas: ...
  metrics: ...

parameters.name: spec.scaleTargetRef
parameters.description: Reference to the scalable workload and the Pods whose metrics are collected.

parameters.name: spec.minReplicas
parameters.description: Smallest allowed replica count. The default is 1.

parameters.name: spec.maxReplicas
parameters.description: Largest allowed replica count.

parameters.name: spec.metrics
parameters.description: Metrics and targets used to calculate the desired replica count.

parameters.name: spec.behavior
parameters.description: Rules for scaling up and down, including policies and stabilization.

HorizontalPodAutoscaler.returns: The HPA status reports current metrics, current replicas, desired replicas, conditions, and the last scale time.

example.title: CPU-based HorizontalPodAutoscaler
example.code:
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: web-hpa
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: web
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: cpu
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 60
example.explanation: This HPA keeps the web Deployment between 2 and 10 Pods and targets 60% average CPU utilization.

useCases.title: CPU-based scaling
useCases.scenario: A web service needs more Pods when average CPU use rises.

useCases.title: Resource and custom metrics
useCases.scenario: A workload must react to memory use or application-specific measurements.

useCases.title: External metric scaling
useCases.scenario: A service should scale from a queue depth or another metric outside the Pods.

interview.question: What are the two main parts of an HPA?
interview.answer: An HPA is an API resource plus a control-plane controller. The resource defines the target and metric rules, while the controller periodically adjusts the target workload's replica count.
interview.followUp: How does the controller find the Pods? It follows scaleTargetRef and uses the target resource's selector labels.

interview.question: How is a resource utilization target calculated?
interview.answer: For a utilization target, the controller compares average Pod usage with the requested resource amount. It uses the resulting ratio to calculate a desired replica count.
interview.followUp: What happens without a CPU or memory request? Utilization for that Pod is undefined, so that metric cannot drive scaling for it.

interview.question: Which metrics can an HPA use?
interview.answer: The stable autoscaling/v2 API supports memory and custom metrics in addition to CPU. The HPA can also use object and external metrics.
interview.followUp: What if several metrics are configured? The controller calculates a recommendation for each and selects the largest desired replica count.

keyPoints: An HPA has a declarative API object and a controller that enforces its desired scaling behavior.
Horizontal scaling adds or removes Pods instead of increasing resources on existing Pods.
scaleTargetRef identifies the workload whose replica count the HPA changes.
Resource metrics come from the resource metrics API; other metric types use custom or external metrics APIs.
With multiple metrics, the HPA uses the highest calculated desired replica count.
The default five-minute downscale stabilization window uses the highest recent recommendation to make scale-down gradual.
gotchas: CPU utilization is undefined for a Pod when a required resource request is missing, so the HPA takes no action for that metric.
Resource-based scaling needs a resource metrics API, commonly provided by Metrics Server, which must be installed separately.
An HPA cannot target workloads such as a DaemonSet because they do not support scaling.
When one metric fails and the available metrics suggest scaling down, the HPA skips the scale-down action.

Ingress.summary: Ingress defines HTTP and HTTPS rules that route external requests to Kubernetes backends. An Ingress controller implements these rules and may provide load balancing, TLS termination, and host-based routing.
Ingress.explanation: An Ingress describes HTTP and HTTPS routing rules. An Ingress controller reads those rules and sends matching requests to Services or other supported backends. It can also provide TLS termination, load balancing, and host-based routing.
Ingress.syntax:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: <name>
spec:
  ingressClassName: <class>
  rules: <host-and-path-rules>
  defaultBackend: <backend>
  tls: <tls-settings>

parameters.name: metadata.name
parameters.description: The Ingress resource name. It must be a valid DNS subdomain name.

parameters.name: spec.ingressClassName
parameters.description: The selected IngressClass resource.

parameters.name: spec.rules
parameters.description: Host and path rules that map requests to backends.

parameters.name: spec.defaultBackend
parameters.description: The backend for requests without a matching rule.

parameters.name: spec.tls
parameters.description: TLS settings for HTTPS termination.

Ingress.returns: The Ingress status reports the current load-balancer state, including ingress hostnames, IP addresses, and ports.

example.title: Route web traffic to a Service
example.code:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
  - host: example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /shop
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: shop
            port:
              number: 80
example.explanation: This sends requests for example.com/shop and its subpaths to port 80 of the shop Service.

useCases.title: Route multiple web services
useCases.scenario: Several web applications share one external entry point and need different host or path routes.

useCases.title: Terminate TLS
useCases.scenario: A cluster needs HTTPS handled at its external frontend.

useCases.title: Provide a default backend
useCases.scenario: Requests need a fallback destination when they match no declared host or path.

interview.question: What is an Ingress?
interview.answer: Ingress is a Kubernetes object that maps incoming HTTP or HTTPS requests to backends. Rules can match a host and a URL path. An Ingress controller implements those rules.
interview.followUp: What happens if no rule matches? The controller may send the request to the configured default backend; behavior can depend on the controller if no default backend is set.

interview.question: Why is an Ingress controller needed?
interview.answer: The controller is required because the Ingress object only declares desired routing. The controller watches Ingress resources and configures a load balancer, proxy, edge router, or other frontend.
interview.followUp: Can different controllers interpret the same Ingress identically? Not always; controller behavior and supported annotations can differ, so its documentation must be checked.

interview.question: How are paths selected?
interview.answer: Prefix matching is case-sensitive and uses path elements separated by slashes. The longest matching path wins, and an Exact match wins over a Prefix match when the paths are otherwise equally matched.
interview.followUp: Does /foo match /foobar with Prefix? No. Prefix matching is element-based, so a partial final-element string is not enough.

keyPoints: The Ingress API is stable starting with Kubernetes 1.19.
Ingress can expose Services, balance requests, terminate TLS, and support name-based virtual hosting.
Use ingressClassName to select the IngressClass that identifies the controller and its configuration.
A request reaches a rule backend only when its host and path match that rule.
A wildcard host must start with *., and it matches one DNS label, not multiple nested labels.
A backend can use either a Service reference or a resource reference, but not both.
gotchas: An Ingress controller must be installed. The resource alone does not route traffic.
Use a NodePort or LoadBalancer Service for traffic other than HTTP and HTTPS.
Mark no more than one IngressClass as the cluster default, or creation without ingressClassName can fail.

Init container.summary: An init container runs to completion before a Pod's app containers start. Multiple init containers run in order, and each must succeed before the next one begins.
Init container.explanation: An init container prepares a Pod before its application containers start. Kubernetes runs init containers in order, waits for each to finish successfully, and retries failures according to the Pod restart policy. After all init containers finish, the application containers start.

parameters.name: spec.initContainers
parameters.description: A list of initialization container definitions in the Pod specification.

parameters.name: spec.restartPolicy
parameters.description: The retry behavior for failed init containers, controlled by the Pod setting.

parameters.name: initContainers[].name
parameters.description: The container name used to select logs and identify status.

Init container.returns: A Pod that proceeds to its app containers after all init containers exit successfully; otherwise it remains initializing or is treated as failed under the documented restart-policy rules.

example.title: Pod with an init container
example.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: init-demo
spec:
  initContainers:
  - name: wait-for-db
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ['sh', '-c', 'until nslookup db; do sleep 2; done']
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ['sh', '-c', 'echo app started; sleep 3600']
example.explanation: The init container waits for the db service. The app container starts only after that command exits successfully.

useCases.title: Wait for a dependency
useCases.scenario: An app needs a database or Service before it starts.

useCases.title: Run setup utilities
useCases.scenario: Startup needs a command-line tool that is not in the app image.

useCases.title: Prepare shared data
useCases.scenario: The app needs generated configuration or files.

useCases.title: Enforce startup conditions
useCases.scenario: A Pod should not start its app until required conditions are true.

interview.question: How does Kubernetes run multiple init containers?
interview.answer: Kubernetes starts init containers before app containers. It runs them in the order listed, and each one must exit successfully before the next starts. If an init container fails, Kubernetes retries it according to the Pod restart policy.
interview.followUp: What happens when restartPolicy is Always? Init containers use OnFailure behavior in that case, so a failed init container is retried until it succeeds.

interview.question: How do you define an init container?
interview.answer: Add an initContainers array to the Pod specification. Each item has the normal container settings, such as an image and command. The app containers are held until every init container completes.
interview.followUp: How can two containers exchange setup data? Mount a shared volume in both containers; an init container can write files that the app container later reads.

interview.question: How do you debug a stuck init container?
interview.answer: Use kubectl get pod to see statuses such as Init:1/2. Use kubectl describe pod for states and restart counts, and kubectl logs POD -c INIT_CONTAINER to inspect a specific init container.
interview.followUp: What does CrashLoopBackOff for an init container suggest? The container is repeatedly failing, so inspect its last state, exit code, events, and logs.

keyPoints: An init container must finish its task; it is not a long-running helper.
Multiple init containers run sequentially in specification order.
A failed init container is retried by the kubelet.
Declare init containers with the Pod's initContainers field.
Init containers can use resources, volumes, and security settings like app containers.
The Pod cannot become Ready while initialization is incomplete.
A Pod restart causes its init-container sequence to run again.
gotchas: Regular init containers cannot use lifecycle hooks or liveness, readiness, and startup probes.
Make init-container actions safe to run more than once.
Ports declared by an init container do not become Service ports.
Use a different name for every app and init container in the Pod.

Job.summary: A Job runs one-off work in Kubernetes. It creates and retries Pods until the required number of successful completions is reached, then stops.
Job.explanation: A Job asks Kubernetes to run one or more Pods until the required number finishes successfully. The Job controller creates or retries Pods, records successful completions, and marks the Job complete when its target is reached.
Job.syntax:
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: <name>
spec:
  template: <pod template>

parameters.name: spec.template
parameters.description: Pod template that defines the Pods created by the Job.

parameters.name: spec.completions
parameters.description: Number of successful completions required for a fixed-count Job.

parameters.name: spec.parallelism
parameters.description: Maximum number of Pods allowed to run at one time.

parameters.name: spec.backoffLimit
parameters.description: Number of retries before the Job is considered failed.

parameters.name: spec.completionMode
parameters.description: Completion behavior: NonIndexed or Indexed.

Job.returns: A completed Job status with successful completions, or a failed Job after its retry limit is reached.

example.title: A simple Job
example.code:
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: pi
spec:
  backoffLimit: 4
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: pi
        image: perl:5.34.0
        command: ["perl", "-Mbignum=bpi", "-wle", "print bpi(2000)"]
example.explanation: This Job runs one Pod that calculates pi and stops after the command finishes.

useCases.title: One-off task
useCases.scenario: Run a command once and retain its completion status.

useCases.title: Fixed completion count
useCases.scenario: Require several successful Pods for one overall task.

useCases.title: Work queue
useCases.scenario: Process work with multiple Pods that coordinate through a shared queue.

useCases.title: Indexed parallel processing
useCases.scenario: Give parallel workers stable indexes for separate pieces of work.

interview.question: What is a Kubernetes Job?
interview.answer: A Job represents work that should finish. Its controller creates Pods and retries them until the requested number of successful completions is reached.
interview.followUp: How does a CronJob differ? A CronJob creates Jobs on a schedule, while a Job runs a task to completion once.

interview.question: How do you run several completions in parallel?
interview.answer: For a fixed completion count, set spec.completions to the required number of successful Pods. You can also set spec.parallelism to limit how many Pods run at once.
interview.followUp: What happens when parallelism is higher than the remaining completions? The actual number of running Pods does not exceed the remaining completions.

interview.question: What is an Indexed Job?
interview.answer: An Indexed Job gives each Pod an index from 0 through completions minus 1. The index is available in the JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX environment variable and other documented Pod metadata.
interview.followUp: Can two Pods temporarily have the same index? Yes. Only the first successful Pod for that index counts, and the controller removes the others when detected.

keyPoints: Use a Job for work that should finish instead of running continuously.
The Job controller creates Pods and retries failed or deleted Pods until the target is met.
The Job becomes complete after the configured number of Pods succeeds.
A Job needs a Pod template under spec.template. The template defines the container and its execution settings.
For one completion, omitting completions and parallelism makes both default to 1.
NonIndexed is the default completion mode and counts successful Pods without assigning work indexes.
Indexed work can read its completion index from the JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX environment variable, a label or annotation, and the Pod hostname.
gotchas: The Pod template must use restartPolicy Never or OnFailure. Other restart policies are invalid for a Job.
Setting parallelism to 0 pauses new work until you raise the value.
Usually leave spec.selector unset. Kubernetes can create the selector for the Job.

interview.question: What does kube-proxy do?
interview.answer: kube-proxy runs on each node and watches Service and EndpointSlice objects. It configures node-level rules that capture traffic for a Service cluster IP and port, then redirects it to an endpoint.
interview.followUp: Why use proxying instead of only DNS round-robin? DNS caching can outlive record TTLs, and some applications resolve names only once. Proxying keeps the virtual address stable while the backend set changes.

interview.question: Which proxy modes are available?
interview.answer: On Linux, kube-proxy supports iptables, IPVS, and nftables modes. On Windows, it uses kernelspace mode.
interview.followUp: What should an upgrade-safe configuration do? Explicitly set the proxy mode instead of relying on the default, because the documented default may change in a future Kubernetes release.

interview.question: What do minSyncPeriod and syncPeriod control?
interview.answer: The minimum sync period limits how often kube-proxy resynchronizes rules after Service or EndpointSlice changes. A zero value can cause an immediate resync for every change, while a larger value can combine changes but delay each one.
interview.followUp: How is this different from syncPeriod? syncPeriod controls broader resynchronization and cleanup work, including noticing interference with the rules.

keyPoints: A kube-proxy process normally runs on every node, unless another component replaces it.
It tracks changes to Services and EndpointSlices from the control plane.
For a Service, it forwards captured traffic to one endpoint, such as a Pod or user-provided IP.
Linux supports iptables, IPVS, and nftables proxy modes.
Windows uses the kernelspace proxy mode.
Nftables is the newer kernel API used by the nftables proxy mode.
gotchas: Do not choose IPVS for new deployments without checking your Kubernetes release plan. The documentation marks this mode as deprecated.
ExternalName Services are not handled by kube-proxy's virtual IP mechanism.
Changing proxy modes can leave kernel rules behind in some cases. Check cleanup behavior before switching modes.

interview.answer: kubectl apply takes a resource definition and makes the cluster match the declared fields. It creates missing resources and updates existing ones.

interview.question: How do you provide input to kubectl apply?
interview.answer: Use -f for a YAML or JSON file, directory, URL, or standard input. Use -k for a directory containing kustomization.yaml.
interview.followUp: How can one input contain several resources? Separate the resource definitions with a document separator: three hyphens on their own line.

interview.question: How is apply different from separate create and update commands?
interview.answer: Apply is declarative: the file describes the desired resource state, so the command chooses whether to create or update the resource. The resource must have a name.
interview.followUp: Why can apply preserve cluster-owned fields? Fields not specified in the resource configuration are left unmodified.

interview.question: How does graceful deletion work?
interview.answer: Graceful deletion gives a supported resource time to stop before forced termination. The default grace period can be changed with --grace-period, and --now sets it to one second.
interview.followUp: What if the resource does not support graceful deletion? The --grace-period option is ignored.

interview.question: What does deletion cascading control?
interview.answer: The --cascade option controls what happens to dependents. Its values are background, orphan, and foreground; background is the default.

interview.answer: kubectl describe prints a detailed view of selected resources and can include related resources such as events or controllers. It is intended for understanding the state of a resource.
interview.followUp: How can you select resources? Use a resource type with a name or name prefix, a label selector, a file, or TYPE/NAME.

interview.question: How does a name prefix work?

interview.question: How do you describe resources in every namespace?

interview.followUp: Can a file be used instead? Yes. Pass the file, directory, or URL with `-f` or `--filename`; use `-R` for recursive directory processing.

interview.question: What does kubectl drain do?
interview.answer: It marks the node unschedulable and evicts or deletes eligible Pods. Eviction is used when the API server supports it; otherwise normal deletion is used. The command waits for graceful termination.
interview.followUp: What can block the operation? PodDisruptionBudgets, unmanaged Pods, and DaemonSet Pods can affect progress; DaemonSet Pods require --ignore-daemonsets and are not deleted.

interview.question: Why does drain skip DaemonSet Pods?
interview.answer: DaemonSet Pods are not deleted because the DaemonSet controller would replace them immediately, and it ignores the node's unschedulable state. Use --ignore-daemonsets to allow the drain to proceed.
interview.followUp: What remains after a successful drain? Mirror Pods and DaemonSet Pods remain, along with any other Pods excluded by the command's rules.

interview.question: How does drain support safe maintenance?
interview.answer: A successful drain safely evicts eligible Pods while respecting their graceful termination period and configured PodDisruptionBudgets. This makes it safe to power down or remove the node for maintenance.
interview.followUp: How can availability be protected? Configure a PodDisruptionBudget before draining applications that need availability.

Mirror Pods are excluded because they cannot be deleted through the API server.
The command does not finish until eligible Pods complete graceful termination.
Eviction respects PodDisruptionBudgets and gives containers time to stop cleanly.
Drain one node per command; separate drain commands may run concurrently for different nodes.
Parallel drains for different nodes still respect the configured PodDisruptionBudget.
gotchas: A node with DaemonSet Pods needs --ignore-daemonsets. The command still leaves those Pods running.
Unmanaged Pods stop the drain unless you explicitly use --force.
Wait for the command to finish before shutting down or servicing the node.
Run kubectl uncordon after maintenance when the node should accept new Pods again.

interview.question: How do you view and stream pod logs?
interview.answer: Use kubectl logs POD for a one-time view. Add -f to keep streaming new log lines, similar to tail -f.
interview.followUp: How do you choose a container? Add -c CONTAINER, or use --all-containers=true to read every container in the pod.

interview.question: How do you inspect logs from a terminated container?
interview.answer: Use -p to show logs from the previous terminated container instance. Select the container with -c when the pod has multiple containers.
interview.followUp: How could you limit the previous output? Combine -p with options such as --tail, --since, or --limit-bytes.

interview.question: How do you collect logs from multiple pods?
interview.answer: Use -l app=nginx to select pods by label. Add --all-containers=true for every container and --max-log-requests=10 to limit concurrent requests.
interview.followUp: What is another way to select many workloads? Use a supported resource such as deployment/nginx or job/hello.

Use -f or --follow to continuously stream new log output.

interview.question: What does kubectl port-forward do?
interview.answer: The command selects a pod and maps a local TCP port to a port in that pod. A resource such as a Deployment or Service can select the pod automatically.
interview.followUp: What happens if the selected pod terminates? The forwarding session ends, so the command must be run again.

interview.question: How do you map ports?
interview.answer: Use the form LOCAL_PORT:REMOTE_PORT, such as 8888:5000. If the local port is omitted, kubectl chooses an available local port.
interview.followUp: Why omit the local port? It avoids managing local port conflicts, although the chosen port is dynamic.

interview.question: Where does kubectl listen?
interview.answer: By default, kubectl listens on localhost. Use --address with comma-separated IP addresses or localhost to choose the listening addresses.
interview.followUp: Can it forward UDP? No. The documented implementation supports TCP ports only.

keyPoints: The command creates local port forwarding to a pod.
A resource type and name can identify the pod source.
If you provide only a resource name, kubectl treats it as a pod name.
For a selector that matches several pods, kubectl picks one automatically.
One command can forward several local and remote ports.
A Service port name can identify the remote target port.
Use an empty local-port position to let kubectl allocate the local port.

This command does not forward UDP traffic.
The command stays attached to the terminal. Use another terminal for the application that uses the forwarded port.
The --address value must contain IP addresses or localhost.

kubectl rollout status.summary: Checks the status of a Kubernetes rollout. It watches the latest rollout until completion by default, but can check immediately, use a timeout, or target a specific revision.

useCases.title: Perform a non-blocking check

useCases.title: Apply a time limit

interview.question: What does kubectl rollout status do?
interview.answer: It reports rollout progress for a resource such as a Deployment. By default, it keeps watching until the rollout finishes.
interview.followUp: How can you avoid waiting? Use --watch=false, or set --timeout to limit how long the watch runs.

interview.question: How do you make the command return without waiting?
interview.answer: Use --watch=false to check without waiting. The command can also use --timeout to stop waiting after a chosen duration.
interview.followUp: What does --timeout=0 mean? It means the watch has no time limit.

interview.question: How do you watch one rollout revision?
interview.answer: Use --revision=N to watch a specific revision. Without that option, the command follows the latest revision, including a newer rollout that starts during the watch.
interview.followUp: Why pin a revision? Pinning lets the command stop if another revision rolls over the revision being checked.

keyPoints: The command displays the status of a rollout.
It watches the latest rollout until it completes unless you change the watch behavior.
Use --revision=N when the status check must target one revision.
The --watch flag controls whether the command continues monitoring until completion.
Use --selector to limit matching resources by labels.
Use --timeout to set how long the command may wait.
gotchas: Without --revision, a new rollout can change which revision the command watches.
The default waits for completion, so use --watch=false when you need an immediate result.
A timeout of zero waits indefinitely; other timeout values need units such as 1s or 2m.

kubectl rollout undo.summary: Roll back a Deployment or another supported workload to an earlier rollout state. By default, it uses the previous known state; --to-revision selects a specific revision.
