interview.question: What is a Pod?
interview.answer: A Pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes. It contains one or more containers that are co-located, co-scheduled, and share network and storage resources.
interview.followUp: Why not put unrelated containers in one Pod? Containers in a Pod are managed as one unit and share resources, so the pattern is best for tightly coupled containers.

interview.question: How do containers in a Pod communicate?
interview.answer: Containers in the same Pod share one network namespace and Pod IP. They can reach each other through localhost, while shared volumes provide a way to exchange data.
interview.followUp: What must containers consider when using localhost? They must use different ports because the network namespace and ports are shared.

interview.question: Why are Pods usually managed by workload resources?
interview.answer: Pods are usually created by workload resources such as Deployments, Jobs, or StatefulSets. Their controllers create replacement Pods, handle replication or rollout, and support automatic healing.
interview.followUp: What happens when a Pod's template changes? Existing Pods are not changed directly; the workload controller creates replacement Pods using the new template.

keyPoints: A Pod is the basic unit Kubernetes deploys and manages.
A Pod contains one or more containers.
Volumes let containers in the same Pod share data.
All containers in a Pod share its IP address and network ports.
Run one application instance per Pod; scale by using more Pods.
Container resource requests help the scheduler choose a node with enough capacity.
Pod status can include resource usage reported by the kubelet.
gotchas: Treat Pods as replaceable units. Use a workload resource to recreate them when needed.
The container list cannot be changed after creation.
Containers in one Pod share a network namespace, so they must coordinate port usage.
For mixed-OS clusters, set a node selector that matches the Pod's operating system.

PodDisruptionBudget.summary: A PodDisruptionBudget limits how many matching Pods may be unavailable during voluntary disruptions. It helps keep a replicated application available during maintenance and other planned actions.
PodDisruptionBudget.explanation: A PodDisruptionBudget limits how many matching Pods may be unavailable during voluntary disruptions. Kubernetes uses the selector to find the Pods and the workload's intended replica count to evaluate whether an eviction can proceed.
PodDisruptionBudget.syntax:
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: <name>
spec:
  selector: <label selector>
  minAvailable: <number or percentage>
  # or maxUnavailable: <number or percentage>

parameters.name: apiVersion
parameters.description: API version of the object.

parameters.name: kind
parameters.description: Resource type. Use PodDisruptionBudget.

parameters.name: metadata
parameters.description: Standard object metadata, such as name and namespace.

parameters.name: spec
parameters.description: Desired PDB behavior, including selector and one availability limit.

parameters.name: status
parameters.description: Latest observed PDB state.

PodDisruptionBudget.returns: The Kubernetes API returns a PodDisruptionBudget object for create, update, and read operations; deletion returns Status.

example.title: A PodDisruptionBudget for a web workload
example.code:
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: web-pdb
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
example.explanation: This budget keeps at least two Pods matching app=web available during voluntary disruption.

useCases.title: Protect replicas during node drain
useCases.scenario: A node is drained for maintenance.

useCases.title: Preserve quorum
useCases.scenario: A quorum-based service needs enough members to continue.

useCases.title: Maintain serving capacity
useCases.scenario: A web service must keep enough replicas serving requests.

interview.question: What does a PodDisruptionBudget control?
interview.answer: A PDB limits simultaneous Pod loss caused by voluntary disruption. It applies to Pods selected by its label selector and is enforced through the Eviction API.
interview.followUp: Can a PDB stop a hardware failure? No. Involuntary disruptions are not prevented, although they count against the budget.

interview.question: How do minAvailable and maxUnavailable differ?
interview.answer: Set either minAvailable or maxUnavailable. minAvailable requires a minimum number or percentage of selected Pods to remain available; maxUnavailable sets the largest allowed unavailable count or percentage.
interview.followUp: What happens if both are set? They are mutually exclusive, so the PDB must use only one.

interview.question: How can you tell whether eviction is currently allowed?
interview.answer: The controller reports disruptionsAllowed and related status values. A disruption is permitted only when the eviction leaves no more than the configured unavailable amount, or preserves the configured minimum.
interview.followUp: What should you check before trusting the status? Confirm observedGeneration equals the PDB object's generation, because status can lag behind the system.

keyPoints: A PDB describes the maximum disruption allowed for a group of Pods.
It protects replicated applications during voluntary disruptions such as maintenance.
The selector identifies which Pods belong to the budget.
maxUnavailable allows eviction when the resulting unavailable count stays within its limit.
minAvailable allows eviction only when the required number or percentage remains available.
The status field disruptionsAllowed shows the current number of permitted disruptions.
gotchas: A PDB cannot stop involuntary failures, but those failures still count against the budget.
Use AlwaysAllow when unhealthy Pods should not block node draining.
Tools should use the Eviction API. Direct deletion can bypass the budget.

Readiness probe.summary: Kubernetes probes let the kubelet check container health. Startup protects slow initialization, liveness triggers restarts for stuck containers, and readiness controls whether Services send traffic.
Readiness probe.explanation: A kubelet runs probes against a container. A startup probe gates the other probes until initialization finishes. A liveness probe detects a container that should be restarted. A readiness probe controls whether the Pod receives Service traffic. Each probe uses one check method: exec, gRPC, HTTP, or TCP.

parameters.name: initialDelaySeconds
parameters.description: Seconds to wait after container start before beginning probes; with a startup probe, liveness and readiness delays begin after startup succeeds.

parameters.name: periodSeconds
parameters.description: Seconds between probe attempts. Default: 10; minimum: 1.

parameters.name: failureThreshold
parameters.description: Consecutive failures required to mark the check failed. Default: 3; minimum: 1.

parameters.name: terminationGracePeriodSeconds
parameters.description: Grace period before forcibly stopping a failed container. The default inherits the Pod value; minimum: 1.

parameters.name: probe mechanism
parameters.description: One probe mechanism: exec, grpc, httpGet, or tcpSocket.

Readiness probe.returns: Probe results are Success, Failure, or Unknown. Success means the diagnostic passed. Failure causes a liveness or startup container restart, or marks a readiness check as not ready. Unknown causes no action and leads to more checks.

example.title: Use all three probe types
example.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: registry.k8s.io/e2e-test-images/agnhost:2.40
    ports:
    - containerPort: 8080
    startupProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /healthz
        port: 8080
      failureThreshold: 30
      periodSeconds: 10
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /healthz
        port: 8080
      periodSeconds: 5
      failureThreshold: 3
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /ready
        port: 8080
      periodSeconds: 5
example.explanation: This Pod allows up to five minutes for startup. After startup succeeds, liveness checks can restart a stuck container, while readiness checks control whether Services send traffic to it.

useCases.title: Protect slow startup
useCases.scenario: The application takes a long time to load data, configuration, or migrations.

useCases.title: Restart a stuck container
useCases.scenario: The process is running but cannot make progress, such as during a deadlock.

useCases.title: Stop traffic without restarting
useCases.scenario: The application is temporarily overloaded or a required backend is unavailable.

useCases.title: Check gRPC health
useCases.scenario: A container exposes a gRPC health-check service.

Readiness probe.since: v1.27 for stable gRPC probes; v1.28 for stable probe-level t

interview.question: What is a startup probe?
interview.answer: A startup probe checks whether the application has finished starting. While it has not succeeded, Kubernetes does not run liveness or readiness probes. If it keeps failing, the kubelet kills the container and applies the restart policy.
interview.followUp: How would you allow five minutes for startup with a ten-second period? Set failureThreshold to 30 and periodSeconds to 10, giving 300 seconds.

interview.question: How do liveness and readiness probes differ?
interview.answer: A liveness probe decides when to restart a container. A readiness probe decides when the container can receive traffic; a failed readiness check leaves the container running but removes it from matching Service endpoints.
interview.followUp: Why use both? Readiness can protect traffic during temporary dependency failures, while liveness can recover an application that is stuck.

interview.question: Which probe mechanisms are available?
interview.answer: A probe must use exactly one mechanism: exec, gRPC, HTTP GET, or TCP socket. Exec succeeds when the command exits with code 0; HTTP succeeds for status codes from 200 through 399; TCP succeeds when the port is open.
interview.followUp: What should an HTTP health endpoint return? It should be a dedicated endpoint with a small response body, because the kubelet stops reading after 10 KiB.

keyPoints: Use a startup probe for containers that need a long initialization period.
Use liveness for failures that indicate the container should be restarted, such as a deadlock.
Use readiness when the application must stay running but should temporarily receive no Service traffic.
A probe selects one check type: exec, gRPC, HTTP GET, or TCP socket.
A failed readiness check removes the Pod from matching Service endpoints without killing its container.
failureThreshold controls how many consecutive failures trigger the failed state.
periodSeconds sets the check interval and defaults to 10 seconds.
gotchas: A bad liveness check can restart containers during high load and cause cascading failures.
Frequent exec checks can add CPU overhead on nodes with many Pods; consider HTTP, TCP, or gRPC when suitable.
Per-probe termination grace periods work for startup and liveness probes, not readiness probes.

ReplicaSet.summary: A ReplicaSet keeps a selected number of identical Pods running. Deployments usually manage ReplicaSets, but you can use one directly when you need simpler or custom control.
ReplicaSet.explanation: A ReplicaSet compares the Pods selected by its label selector with the desired replica count. It creates Pods from its template when there are too few and removes excess Pods when there are too many. It tracks owned Pods through ownerReferences.
ReplicaSet.syntax:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: ReplicaSet
metadata:
  name: <name>
spec:
  replicas: <number>
  selector:
    matchLabels: <labels>
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: <matching-labels>
    spec: <pod-spec>

parameters.name: spec.selector
parameters.description: Label selector used to find Pods that the ReplicaSet controls. It must match the template labels.

parameters.name: spec.replicas
parameters.description: Desired number of non-terminating Pods.

parameters.name: spec.template
parameters.description: Pod definition used when the ReplicaSet needs to create a Pod.

parameters.name: spec.minReadySeconds
parameters.description: Minimum time a newly created Pod must be ready before it counts as available.

ReplicaSet.returns: A ReplicaSet resource with observed status, including replica counts, available and ready Pods, conditions, and observed generation.

example.title: Create a ReplicaSet
example.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: ReplicaSet
metadata:
  name: frontend
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      tier: frontend
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        tier: frontend
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: nginx:1.27
example.explanation: This manifest creates a ReplicaSet that keeps three Pods with the tier=frontend label running.

useCases.title: Maintain availability
useCases.scenario: Keep a fixed number of interchangeable application Pods running.

useCases.title: Autoscale replicas
useCases.scenario: Let an HPA adjust the number of Pods from workload metrics.

useCases.title: Isolate a Pod for debugging
useCases.scenario: Remove a Pod from the ReplicaSet temporarily by changing its labels.

interview.question: What does a ReplicaSet do?
interview.answer: A ReplicaSet maintains a target number of Pods. It selects Pods by labels, creates missing Pods from its template, and removes excess Pods.
interview.followUp: How does it know which Pods it owns? It uses ownerReferences on acquired Pods and the selector to find matching Pods that have no controller owner.

interview.question: What are the main fields in a ReplicaSet specification?
interview.answer: The selector identifies Pods that the ReplicaSet controls. The template labels must match the selector, and the replica count sets the desired number of Pods.
interview.followUp: What happens if matching, unowned Pods already exist? The ReplicaSet can adopt them, so bare Pods should not use labels selected by an existing ReplicaSet.

interview.question: Why use a Deployment instead of a ReplicaSet?
interview.answer: A Deployment is preferred because it manages ReplicaSets and supports declarative, server-side rolling updates. Direct ReplicaSet use is mainly for cases needing custom update control or no updates.
interview.followUp: What happens when a ReplicaSet is deleted? By default, garbage collection deletes its dependent Pods; an orphan propagation policy can leave the Pods running.

keyPoints: A ReplicaSet keeps a stable set of identical Pods available.
The controller creates or deletes Pods to reach the configured replica count.
The label selector determines which existing Pods the ReplicaSet can acquire.
Matching Pods without a controller owner can be adopted automatically.
If replicas is omitted, the desired count is one Pod.
An HPA can change a ReplicaSet's replica count based on metrics such as CPU use.
gotchas: Do not reuse labels that another controller selects. Controllers may try to adopt the same Pods.
The template labels must satisfy the selector. Otherwise, Kubernetes rejects the ReplicaSet.
A ReplicaSet Pod template can use only the Always restart policy.
Use a Deployment for controlled Pod updates. A ReplicaSet does not provide rolling updates itself.

Requests and limits.summary: A LimitRange sets per-object resource rules inside one namespace. It can enforce minimums and maximums, provide default requests and limits, and constrain storage requests.
Requests and limits.explanation: A LimitRange sets per-object resource rules inside one namespace. It can require minimums and maximums, provide default requests and limits, and constrain storage requests. It does not change objects that already exist.
Requests and limits.syntax:
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: NAME
  namespace: NAMESPACE
spec:
  limits:
  - type: Container
    min: RESOURCE_AMOUNTS
    max: RESOURCE_AMOUNTS
    default: RESOURCE_AMOUNTS
    defaultRequest: RESOURCE_AMOUNTS

example.title: A namespace LimitRange
example.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: compute-limits
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  limits:
  - type: Container
    default:
      cpu: "500m"
      memory: "256Mi"
    defaultRequest:
      cpu: "200m"
      memory: "128Mi"
    max:
      cpu: "1"
      memory: "512Mi"
    min:
      cpu: "100m"
      memory: "64Mi"
example.explanation: This policy gives containers default CPU and memory values and sets minimum and maximum values in the namespace.

useCases.title: Set per-container bounds
useCases.scenario: A namespace has many teams and each container must declare safe CPU and memory bounds.

useCases.title: Add default requests and limits
useCases.scenario: Workloads often omit resource values and need predictable admission defaults.

useCases.title: Constrain PVC storage
useCases.scenario: PVCs in a namespace must stay within approved storage sizes.

interview.question: How does a LimitRange differ from a ResourceQuota?
interview.answer: A LimitRange applies resource constraints to objects in one namespace. It can set minimum and maximum CPU or memory values per container or Pod, and it can set defaults. A ResourceQuota instead limits aggregate consumption or object counts in a namespace.
interview.followUp: What happens to objects created before the policy changes? They are not changed; the new rules apply during admission to later objects.

interview.question: What are requests and limits used for?
interview.answer: Requests tell the scheduler how much resource to reserve for placement, while limits cap or constrain runtime use. A LimitRange can supply defaults when a workload omits these values.
interview.followUp: What happens when only a limit is specified? If no admission-time default request exists, Kubernetes copies the limit into the request.

interview.question: What resources can a LimitRange constrain?
interview.answer: A LimitRange is scoped to a namespace and can constrain each applicable object, such as a Pod, container, or PersistentVolumeClaim. For storage, it can enforce minimum and maximum PVC requests.
interview.followUp: Does the policy itself guarantee that the namespace has enough total capacity? No. Aggregate capacity is handled by ResourceQuota and node scheduling.

keyPoints: A LimitRange controls the requests and limits that objects may declare.
It can set CPU and memory minimums and maximums for a Pod or container.
It can restrict the requested storage size of PersistentVolumeClaims.
A ResourceQuota controls the namespace total, while a LimitRange controls individual objects.
gotchas: Changing a LimitRange does not update existing Pods or containers.
When a limit is set without a request, Kubernetes may use the limit as the request if no admission mechanism supplies a default.
Namespace quotas and per-object limits can still prevent a new Pod or container from being created.

ResourceQuota.summary: A ResourceQuota limits aggregate resource use in a namespace. It can also limit how many objects of selected API kinds users can create.
ResourceQuota.explanation: A ResourceQuota limits the combined resource use of objects in one namespace. It can limit CPU, memory, object counts, and other supported resources. Kubernetes rejects a new or changed object when it would exceed a hard limit.
ResourceQuota.syntax:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: <name>
  namespace: <namespace>
spec:
  hard:
    <resource>: <limit>

parameters.name: metadata.namespace
parameters.description: The namespace containing the quota and the objects it tracks.

parameters.name: spec.hard
parameters.description: Desired hard limits for named resources.

parameters.name: spec.scopeSelector
parameters.description: Optional scope filters that select which objects count.

parameters.name: spec.scopes
parameters.description: Optional list of scopes that must match tracked objects.

ResourceQuota.returns: The ResourceQuota status reports enforced hard limits in status.hard and current namespace usage in status.used.

example.title: CPU and memory quota
example.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: compute-resources
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "1"
    requests.memory: 1Gi
    limits.cpu: "2"
    limits.memory: 2Gi
example.explanation: This quota limits the total CPU and memory requests and limits for Pods in the team-a namespace.

useCases.title: Set namespace resource budgets
useCases.scenario: Several teams share a cluster and need separate CPU and memory budgets.

useCases.title: Limit object counts
useCases.scenario: A namespace must not create too many Pods, Secrets, or Services.

useCases.title: Apply scoped quotas
useCases.scenario: Only Pods with a selected priority class or QoS scope should consume a quota.

interview.question: What does a ResourceQuota control?
interview.answer: A ResourceQuota sets aggregate limits for resources in a namespace. It can track compute resources such as CPU and memory, or object counts such as Pods and Services.
interview.followUp: How can quotas affect a Deployment? The Deployment object may be created, but some of its Pods may fail to be created when quota is insufficient.

interview.question: What happens when a request exceeds quota?
interview.answer: Kubernetes tracks usage against the quota's hard limits. If a create or update would exceed a limit, the control plane rejects the request with HTTP 403 Forbidden.
interview.followUp: What happens to existing objects after a quota change? Existing resources are not affected by contention or quota changes.

interview.question: What Pod fields may be required by a CPU or memory quota?
interview.answer: CPU and memory quotas require every new Pod to specify requests or limits for the enforced resource. A LimitRange can provide default requests for these values.
interview.followUp: Do all quota-managed resources require requests or limits? No. For other resources, Pods without a request or limit for that resource can be ignored by the quota.

keyPoints: A ResourceQuota limits the combined resource consumption of objects in one namespace.
It can cap object counts by API kind, such as Pods, Secrets, or Services.
Scopes narrow which objects count toward a quota; all listed scope conditions must match.
The ResourceQuota name must follow DNS subdomain naming rules.
Quota enforcement starts when a ResourceQuota exists in the namespace.
A hard requests.memory value limits the sum of memory requests across the namespace.
gotchas: Changing a quota does not change resources that already exist.
A request that would exceed quota is rejected with HTTP 403.
Adding nodes does not automatically increase a namespace's quota.

Role.summary: A Role is a namespaced set of permission rules. A RoleBinding can grant those rules to users or other subjects in that namespace.
Role.explanation: A Role groups permission rules inside one namespace. A RoleBinding can refer to the Role and grant its rules to users or other subjects. Each rule states which actions are allowed on which resources, API groups, subresources, or named resources.

parameters.name: NAME
parameters.description: The Role name in kubectl create role NAME.

parameters.name: --verb
parameters.description: Actions allowed by the rule, such as get, list, or watch.

parameters.name: --resource
parameters.description: Resource targeted by the rule, optionally with an API group or subresource.

parameters.name: --resource-name
parameters.description: Specific resource names allowed by the rule.

Role.returns: The Kubernetes API returns a Role for a successful create, read, replace, or patch operation. Listing returns a RoleList.

example.title: Create a Pod reader role
example.code: kubectl create role pod-reader --verb=get --verb=list --verb=watch --resource=pods
example.explanation: Creates a namespaced Role named pod-reader that permits reading Pod objects.

useCases.title: Namespace-scoped access
useCases.scenario: Give a user or service account limited access inside one namespace.

useCases.title: Read-only permissions
useCases.scenario: Allow read access to selected Pods or other resources.

useCases.title: Named-resource access
useCases.scenario: Limit access to named resources rather than every resource of a type.

interview.question: What is a Kubernetes Role?
interview.answer: A Role is a namespaced collection of PolicyRules. A RoleBinding can reference it as one permission unit.
interview.followUp: How would you grant the same permissions across namespaces? Use a ClusterRole, then create bindings in the required namespaces.

interview.question: How do you create a Role from the command line?
interview.answer: Use kubectl create role NAME with one or more --verb flags and a --resource flag. For example, --verb=get --resource=pods permits the get action on Pods.
interview.followUp: How can the rule target only selected objects? Add --resource-name once for each allowed resource name.

interview.question: How are Roles read and listed through the API?
interview.answer: A RoleList contains multiple Role objects. Namespaced listing uses /apis/rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1/namespaces/{namespace}/roles, while an all-namespaces list uses /apis/rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1/roles.
interview.followUp: How can a client receive changes instead of a single list? Set watch=true and provide a resourceVersion.

keyPoints: A Role stores permission rules for one namespace.
The rules field contains every permission rule in the Role.
A RoleBinding assigns the Role's permissions to subjects in the namespace.
The --resource option chooses the resource affected by a command-created rule.
Use --resource-name to restrict a rule to specific resource names.
The command syntax supports a verb and a resource, including an API group or subresource.
gotchas: A Role is limited to one namespace and does not grant permissions by itself. A RoleBinding is needed to assign its rules.
The kind identifies the object type and cannot be changed after creation.
With --dry-run=client, kubectl prints the object and does not send it to the API server.

RoleBinding.summary: A RoleBinding gives users, groups, or service accounts the permissions from a Role or ClusterRole. Its namespace controls where those permissions work.
RoleBinding.explanation: A RoleBinding grants an existing Role or ClusterRole to users, groups, or service accounts. Its namespace limits where the permissions apply, and roleRef identifies the role. The roleRef cannot be changed after creation; delete and recreate the binding to use another role.

parameters.name: namespace
parameters.description: The namespace containing the RoleBinding and limiting its effect.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: The RoleBinding name.

parameters.name: subjects
parameters.description: Users, groups, or service accounts receiving the permissions.

parameters.name: roleRef
parameters.description: The referenced Role or ClusterRole; this field is immutable.

RoleBinding.returns: RoleBinding objects for create, read, and update operations; RoleBindingList for list operations.

example.title: Bind a Role to a user
example.code:
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: read-pods
  namespace: default
subjects:
- kind: User
  name: jane
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: pod-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
example.explanation: This binds the existing pod-reader Role to jane in the default namespace.

useCases.title: Namespace user access
useCases.scenario: Give one namespace access to a user

useCases.title: Shared ClusterRole
useCases.scenario: Reuse one common permission set in several namespaces

useCases.title: Service account access
useCases.scenario: Grant permissions to an application identity

interview.question: What does a RoleBinding do?
interview.answer: A RoleBinding connects subjects to a Role or ClusterRole. It grants access only in the RoleBinding's namespace.
interview.followUp: How can one shared role be reused in many namespaces? Create one ClusterRole, then create a separate RoleBinding in each namespace.

interview.question: Can a RoleBinding reference a ClusterRole?
interview.answer: A RoleBinding can reference a Role in its own namespace or a ClusterRole. A ClusterRole reference still grants permissions only inside the RoleBinding's namespace.
interview.followUp: How do you grant the same access across the whole cluster? Use a ClusterRoleBinding instead.

interview.question: Can you change the role after creating a RoleBinding?
interview.answer: The roleRef field is immutable. Kubernetes rejects an update that changes it, so the binding must be deleted and recreated.
interview.followUp: Why enforce this rule? It lets someone manage subjects without silently changing the permissions granted by the binding.

keyPoints: It assigns permissions from an existing role to one or more subjects.
Subjects can be users, groups, or service accounts.
A namespaced RoleBinding can use a Role from its own namespace.
It can reuse a cluster-wide role definition without granting cluster-wide access.
The subjects list identifies the accounts that receive the role's permissions.
gotchas: roleRef cannot be edited after creation. Replace the RoleBinding if it must refer to a different role.
A RoleBinding does not grant access in other namespaces, even when it refers to a ClusterRole.
Do not accidentally create user or group names that start with system:.

Rolling update.summary: A Kubernetes Deployment can replace old Pods with new Pods gradually. This rolling update keeps the application available while the new version starts.
Rolling update.explanation: A Deployment replaces old Pods with new Pods when its Pod template changes. During a RollingUpdate, Kubernetes scales the new ReplicaSet up and the old ReplicaSet down in stages. The update can be watched, paused, resumed, or rolled back.
Rolling update.syntax:
kubectl set image deployment/<deployment-name> <container-name>=<image>
kubectl rollout status deployment/<deployment-name>
kubectl rollout pause deployment/<deployment-name>
kubectl rollout resume deployment/<deployment-name>
kubectl rollout undo deployment/<deployment-name>

parameters.name: maxUnavailable
parameters.description: Maximum desired Pods that may be unavailable during an update. It can be an absolute number or a percentage.

parameters.name: maxSurge
parameters.description: Maximum Pods that may be created above the desired count. It can be an absolute number or a percentage.

parameters.name: revisionHistoryLimit
parameters.description: Number of old ReplicaSets retained for possible rollback; the default is 10.

example.title: Update an image
example.code:
kubectl set image deployment/nginx-deployment nginx=nginx:1.16.1
kubectl rollout status deployment/nginx-deployment
kubectl get deployment nginx-deployment
example.explanation: This changes the container image, waits for the rollout to finish, and checks the Deployment.

useCases.title: Deploy a new version
useCases.scenario: Release a new container image while keeping the application available.

useCases.title: Pause a rollout
useCases.scenario: Inspect an update after only part of the new version is running.

useCases.title: Recover from a bad update
useCases.scenario: Return to a previous working ReplicaSet after a failed release.

interview.question: What triggers a rolling update?
interview.answer: A change to .spec.template starts a rolling update. Kubernetes creates a new ReplicaSet, gradually adds its Pods, and removes Pods from the old ReplicaSet.
interview.followUp: What happens if another update arrives during the rollout? Kubernetes creates a newer ReplicaSet and scales down the ReplicaSet from the earlier rollout.

interview.question: What do maxUnavailable and maxSurge control?
interview.answer: maxUnavailable limits how many desired Pods may be unavailable. maxSurge limits how many Pods may exist above the desired count. Both accept numbers or percentages.
interview.followUp: How are percentages converted? maxUnavailable rounds down, while maxSurge rounds up.

interview.question: How do you roll back a Deployment?
interview.answer: Use kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name> to return to the previous revision. The Deployment keeps old ReplicaSets according to revisionHistoryLimit, which defaults to 10.
interview.followUp: Can rollback be disabled? Yes. Setting .spec.revisionHistoryLimit to 0 disables rollback.

keyPoints: Changing the Pod template starts a rolling update.
Run rollout status to monitor whether the update finishes.
While paused, multiple changes can be grouped into one rollout.
RollingUpdate is the default strategy and replaces Pods gradually.
Recreate causes downtime because old Pods are removed before new Pods start.
Both maxUnavailable and maxSurge default to 25% for RollingUpdate.
gotchas: Do not set both maxUnavailable and maxSurge to zero.
Terminating Pods can make the total Pod count and resource use temporarily higher than expected.
A revisionHistoryLimit of 0 removes the ability to roll back.

Scheduler.summary: kube-scheduler assigns unscheduled Pods to Nodes. It filters unsuitable Nodes, scores the feasible ones, and binds each Pod to the highest-scoring Node.
Scheduler.explanation: kube-scheduler watches for Pods without a Node. It filters out Nodes that cannot meet the Pod's requirements, scores the remaining feasible Nodes, and binds the Pod to the highest-scoring Node. You can change this behavior with profiles and plugins at scheduling extension points.

parameters.name: --config
parameters.description: Path to a KubeSchedulerConfiguration file.

parameters.name: spec.schedulerName
parameters.description: Name of the scheduler profile selected by a Pod.

Scheduler.returns: A binding decision that assigns the Pod to a selected Node.

example.title: Configure a scheduler profile
example.code:
apiVersion: kubescheduler.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: KubeSchedulerConfiguration
profiles:
  - schedulerName: no-scoring-scheduler
    plugins:
      preScore:
        disabled:
          - name: '*'
      score:
        disabled:
          - name: '*'
example.explanation: This profile disables all pre-scoring and scoring plugins. A Pod can select it with spec.schedulerName: no-scoring-scheduler.

useCases.title: Multiple scheduler profiles
useCases.scenario: Use different scheduling behavior for different workloads in one scheduler process.

useCases.title: Customize scheduling
useCases.scenario: Change filtering or scoring behavior with built-in or custom plugins.

useCases.title: Choose a profile with schedulerName
useCases.scenario: Select a particular scheduler profile for a Pod.

interview.question: How does kube-scheduler choose a Node?
interview.answer: The scheduler first filters Nodes that cannot satisfy the Pod's requirements. It then scores the feasible Nodes and binds the Pod to the Node with the highest score; equal top scores are resolved randomly.
interview.followUp: What happens if filtering removes every Node? The Pod remains unscheduled until a suitable Node becomes available.

interview.question: What is a scheduling profile?
interview.answer: A scheduling profile configures scheduler stages through extension points. Plugins implement behaviors such as queue sorting, filtering, scoring, reserving, permitting, pre-binding, and binding.
interview.followUp: How can a Pod select a profile? Set its spec.schedulerName to the profile's unique scheduler name.

interview.question: Why use multiple scheduler profiles?
interview.answer: Multiple profiles let one kube-scheduler process use different plugin configurations. Each profile needs a unique scheduler name, and Pods select the desired profile through spec.schedulerName.
interview.followUp: What shared constraint applies to profiles? They must use the same queueSort plugin and configuration because they share one pending-Pod queue.

keyPoints: kube-scheduler watches for newly created Pods that do not yet have a Node.
A feasible Node satisfies the scheduling requirements of the Pod.
Filtering removes Nodes that cannot run the Pod.
Scoring ranks the Nodes that pass filtering.
The scheduler selects the highest-ranked Node.
Plugins add scheduling behavior by implementing extension points.
gotchas: A custom profile is not used unless the Pod sets spec.schedulerName to that profile's scheduler name. Pods without that field use default-scheduler.
Multiple profiles share one pending-Pod queue, so every profile must use the same queueSort plugin and matching configuration.
A Pod stays unscheduled when filtering finds no feasible Node.

Secret.summary: A Kubernetes Secret stores small sensitive values such as passwords, tokens, and keys. Pods can use Secrets as environment variables or mounted files.
Secret.explanation: A Secret is a Kubernetes object for small sensitive values such as passwords, tokens, and keys. Pods can use it as environment variables or mounted files. The data field uses base64 strings, while stringData accepts plain text during creation or updates.
Secret.syntax:
kubectl create secret generic NAME

apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: NAME
data: {}
stringData: {}

parameters.name: apiVersion
parameters.description: The resource API version. For Secrets, the manifest uses v1.

parameters.name: kind
parameters.description: The object type. For this resource, use Secret.

parameters.name: metadata
parameters.description: Object metadata, including the Secret name and namespace.

parameters.name: data
parameters.description: Base64-encoded arbitrary Secret values.

parameters.name: stringData
parameters.description: Plain-text input values that Kubernetes merges into data.

parameters.name: type
parameters.description: Optional type used to describe the Secret and support type-specific handling.

parameters.name: immutable
parameters.description: Optional flag that prevents later data updates when true.

Secret.returns: A Kubernetes Secret object. API create operations can return HTTP 200, 201, or 202; read operations return the Secret with HTTP 200.

example.title: Create a Secret from YAML
example.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: app-secret
type: Opaque
stringData:
  username: admin
  password: change-me
example.explanation: This manifest creates an Opaque Secret. stringData accepts plain strings, and Kubernetes stores them in data as base64 values.

useCases.title: Provide application credentials
useCases.scenario: A container needs a password, token, or key at runtime.

useCases.title: Store image pull credentials
useCases.scenario: A Pod must authenticate to a private container registry.

useCases.title: Provide authentication material
useCases.scenario: A program needs an SSH private key or TLS data.

useCases.title: Mount dotfiles
useCases.scenario: A volume should contain a hidden dotfile.

interview.question: What is a Kubernetes Secret?
interview.answer: A Secret stores small sensitive values, such as passwords, tokens, or keys. A Pod can consume those values through environment variables or mounted files.
interview.followUp: How should Secret storage be protected? Enable encryption at rest, apply least-privilege RBAC, restrict access to specific containers, and consider an external Secret store.

interview.question: What is the difference between data and stringData?
interview.answer: data contains base64-encoded values. stringData accepts unencoded strings as a write-only convenience field, and Kubernetes converts them into data.
interview.followUp: What happens when both fields contain the same key? The stringData value wins.

interview.question: Which Secret types does Kubernetes provide?
interview.answer: Opaque is the default type for arbitrary user-defined data. Kubernetes also defines types for registry credentials, basic authentication, SSH authentication, TLS, and ServiceAccount tokens.
interview.followUp: Which ServiceAccount token method is recommended for new workloads? Use the TokenRequest API or projected tokens to obtain short-lived, automatically rotating credentials.

keyPoints: Use Secrets for small sensitive values instead of placing them in application code, Pod specifications, or container images.
Put encoded values in data. Each key may contain letters, numbers, a hyphen, an underscore, or a period.
Use stringData when a manifest needs to provide ordinary text without manually encoding it.
Choose Secret for confidential values and ConfigMap for non-confidential configuration.
A container can receive Secret values through environment variables or through a mounted Secret volume.
Set immutable to true when Secret data must not change; metadata can still be modified.
A Secret has a limit on the combined size of values in its data field.
gotchas: Base64 encoding does not provide encryption. Enable encryption at rest and limit access with least-privilege RBAC.
Allowing Pod creation can indirectly grant access to Secrets in the same namespace.
Avoid relying on stringData with server-side apply.
If the same key exists in data and stringData, the stringData value replaces the data value.

Service.summary: A Kubernetes Service gives clients a stable network endpoint for a changing group of Pods. It uses selectors and EndpointSlices to route traffic to matching backends.
Service.explanation: A Service gives clients one stable way to reach a changing group of Pods. A selector finds matching Pods, and Kubernetes updates EndpointSlices as those Pods change. The Service can expose a different client port from the port used by the Pods.
Service.syntax:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: <name>
spec:
  selector: <label-selector>
  ports:
    - port: <service-port>
      targetPort: <pod-port>

parameters.name: spec.selector
parameters.description: The label selector that chooses Pods for the Service.

parameters.name: spec.ports
parameters.description: The ports exposed by the Service.

parameters.name: spec.type
parameters.description: The Service exposure mode, such as ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer, or ExternalName.

parameters.name: spec.ports[].targetPort
parameters.description: The port on which a selected Pod receives traffic.

Service.returns: A network endpoint for reaching the selected backend Pods, plus EndpointSlices that describe those backends.

example.title: Expose Pods with a Service
example.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-service
spec:
  selector:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: MyApp
  ports:
    - name: http
      protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 9376
example.explanation: This creates a Service named my-service. It sends TCP traffic from port 80 to port 9376 on matching Pods.

useCases.title: Stable access to changing Pods
useCases.scenario: A Deployment replaces Pods while keeping the application available.

useCases.title: External or partially migrated backends
useCases.scenario: A test or migration environment must reach a database or backend outside Kubernetes.

useCases.title: Multiple service ports
useCases.scenario: One application needs HTTP and HTTPS or other listeners.

useCases.title: HTTP entry through Ingress
useCases.scenario: A web workload needs routing rules for several components behind one listener.

Service.since: v1.21 for stable EndpointSlices; v1.20 for stable appProtoco

interview.question: What problem does a Kubernetes Service solve?
interview.answer: A Service is an abstraction that exposes one or more Pods through a stable network endpoint. Its selector chooses the Pods, while Kubernetes maintains EndpointSlices for the matching endpoints.
interview.followUp: How can a Service target systems outside the cluster? Define it without a selector and create an EndpointSlice that lists the external addresses and ports.

interview.question: How does a Service find its backends?
interview.answer: ClusterIP exposes a Service only inside the cluster and is the default type. NodePort also exposes it through a port on each node. Other types can provide external access, depending on the configured Service type and infrastructure.
interview.followUp: When would you use a Service without a selector? Use one when the backend is external, in another namespace or cluster, or only partly migrated to Kubernetes.

interview.question: What is the role of a selector and EndpointSlice?
interview.answer: A selector matches Pod labels. The Service controller watches matching Pods and updates the Service's EndpointSlices when the backend set changes.
interview.followUp: Why prefer EndpointSlices over Endpoints? EndpointSlices support dual-stack clusters and newer features, while the older Endpoints API is deprecated and can truncate large endpoint lists.

keyPoints: A Service is a Kubernetes object that you create and change through the Kubernetes API.
A selector normally chooses backend Pods by matching their labels.
A normal Service receives a cluster IP that clients use as its virtual address.
The Service port and the Pod target port can have different values.
TCP is the default protocol, but supported alternatives can be configured.
EndpointSlices store the backend endpoints in manageable groups.
gotchas: The Service name must follow RFC 1123 label rules.
Name every port when the Service exposes more than one port.
A Service without a selector needs manually managed EndpointSlices.

ServiceAccount.summary: A ServiceAccount is a namespaced identity for processes running in Kubernetes Pods. Use it with RBAC to control API access and with Pod settings to provide credentials.
ServiceAccount.explanation: A ServiceAccount gives a process an identity in a Kubernetes cluster. Create it in a namespace, grant it permissions with RBAC, and assign it to a Pod with spec.serviceAccountName; Kubernetes can then provide a short-lived, rotating token through a projected volume.
ServiceAccount.syntax:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: <name>
  namespace: <namespace>

parameters.name: apiVersion
parameters.description: API version of the object.

parameters.name: automountServiceAccountToken
parameters.description: Whether Pods using this account receive an API token automatically. A Pod setting can override it.

parameters.name: imagePullSecrets
parameters.description: References to Secrets in the same namespace for pulling images.

parameters.name: metadata
parameters.description: Standard Kubernetes object metadata, including name and namespace.

ServiceAccount.returns: A ServiceAccount object for create, read, replace, or patch operations; list operations return ServiceAccountList.

example.title: Create a ServiceAccount
example.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: app-reader
  namespace: default
automountServiceAccountToken: false
imagePullSecrets:
  - name: private-registry
example.explanation: This manifest creates a namespaced ServiceAccount, disables automatic token mounting for Pods that use it, and names a registry Secret for image pulls.

useCases.title: Give a workload API access
useCases.scenario: A Pod must read selected Kubernetes resources.

useCases.title: Authenticate to an external service
useCases.scenario: A workload needs a trusted identity for a cloud or other external API.

useCases.title: Configure private image pulls
useCases.scenario: A Pod pulls an image from a private registry.

useCases.title: Authenticate external automation
useCases.scenario: A CI/CD system outside the cluster must authenticate to the Kubernetes API.

ServiceAccount.since: v1.22 for projected, short-lived ServiceAccount token volume

interview.question: What is a Kubernetes ServiceAccount?
interview.answer: A ServiceAccount is a namespaced identity for processes running in Pods. A Pod uses it to authenticate to the Kubernetes API server or to another system that trusts its tokens.
interview.followUp: How would you limit its access? Create an RBAC Role with only the required permissions, then bind that Role to the ServiceAccount with a RoleBinding.

interview.question: How does a Pod use a ServiceAccount?
interview.answer: Set spec.serviceAccountName in the Pod specification. Kubernetes then supplies credentials for that account, normally as a projected volume containing a short-lived token obtained through the TokenRequest API.
interview.followUp: How can you stop this automatic credential injection? Set automountServiceAccountToken: false in the Pod specification, or on the ServiceAccount when appropriate.

interview.question: How are ServiceAccount tokens handled?
interview.answer: Current Kubernetes versions use time-limited projected tokens that the kubelet refreshes before expiry. These tokens are bound to the Pod and use the Kubernetes API server as their audience.
interview.followUp: Why is TokenReview preferred for validating these tokens? It can reject tokens bound to deleted API objects, while direct OIDC validation may accept them until expiration.

keyPoints: Kubernetes creates a ServiceAccount named default in each namespace.
The same ServiceAccount name can exist in different namespaces, and each object has a separate identity.
Set a Pod's spec.serviceAccountName to select the account used by its processes.
Use RBAC Roles and bindings to give the account only the actions its workload requires.
The kubelet obtains a temporary token and refreshes it before the token expires.
Use imagePullSecrets for registry credentials; they are used by the kubelet for image pulls rather than mounted into the Pod.
gotchas: Do not assume the default ServiceAccount can perform useful API actions. Grant only the permissions the workload needs.
Prefer TokenRequest tokens over manually created Secret tokens. Secret-based tokens do not expire or rotate.
Do not use this annotation for new designs. Use separate namespaces to isolate access to mounted Secrets.

Sidecar container.summary: A Kubernetes sidecar is a helper container that runs in the same Pod as the main application. Define a native sidecar in initContainers with restartPolicy: Always so it follows init ordering but keeps running with the app.
Sidecar container.explanation: Kubernetes implements a native sidecar as an init container with restartPolicy: Always. It starts during Pod setup, remains running with the application, and follows init-container ordering. Kubernetes stops sidecars after the main containers and shuts them down in reverse declaration order.

example.title: Deployment with a native sidecar
example.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: myapp
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: myapp
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: myapp
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: alpine:latest
        command: ["sh", "-c", "echo log >> /data/log.txt; sleep 3600"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /data
      initContainers:
      - name: logger
        image: alpine:latest
        restartPolicy: Always
        command: ["sh", "-c", "tail -F /data/log.txt"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /data
      volumes:
      - name: data
        emptyDir: {}
example.explanation: This Deployment puts the application in containers and the logger in initContainers. The logger becomes a sidecar because its restartPolicy is Always. Both containers use the same emptyDir volume.

useCases.title: Log shipping
useCases.scenario: An application writes files that another process must read and forward.

useCases.title: Supporting services
useCases.scenario: A helper must provide monitoring, security, or another supporting service without changing app code.

useCases.title: Ordered initialization with a long-running helper
useCases.scenario: A Pod needs ordered startup, while a helper must remain available afterward.

interview.question: How does Kubernetes define a native sidecar?
interview.answer: A native sidecar is declared in spec.initContainers with restartPolicy: Always. Unlike a regular init container, it continues running after startup and can support the main application.
interview.followUp: How are multiple sidecars stopped? They are stopped after the main containers, in reverse order from their appearance in the Pod specification.

interview.question: How do native sidecars affect Pod startup?
interview.answer: Native sidecars follow init-container ordering, so later init containers wait until the sidecar has started. A readiness probe on the sidecar can also affect whether the Pod is ready.
interview.followUp: What happens if a sidecar has a startup probe? Kubernetes considers it started after the startup probe succeeds, allowing the next init container to start.

interview.question: How do native sidecars work with Jobs?
interview.answer: A Job can complete when its main container finishes even if its native sidecar is still running. This avoids leaving the Job incomplete because a supporting sidecar continues to run.
interview.followUp: What is one benefit over a regular-container sidecar in a Job? Native sidecars do not block completion when the Job uses OnFailure or Never as its Pod restart policy.

keyPoints: A sidecar is a helper container in the same Pod as the main application.
Native sidecars use the initContainers list, but they keep running after initialization.
Set restartPolicy: Always on an init container to make it a native sidecar.
A sidecar readiness probe can control the Pod's ready state.
During termination, sidecars stop in reverse declaration order after the app containers stop.
Scheduling uses the greater of total app-sidecar resources or the effective init-container resource for each resource.
gotchas: A sidecar is not a regular init container. It keeps running after startup and shares the Pod's network namespace with the app.
Changing the sidecar image restarts that container, but does not restart the whole Pod.
A sidecar may be force-killed during Pod termination if other containers use the available grace period.

Startup probe.sourceTitle: Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes | Kubernetes
Startup probe.summary: A startup probe checks whether a container's application has finished starting. Kubernetes waits for it to succeed before running liveness or readiness probes.
Startup probe.explanation: A startup probe checks whether a container's application has finished starting. Until it succeeds, Kubernetes does not run that container's liveness or readiness probes. If it keeps failing, the kubelet restarts the container according to the Pod's restart policy.
Startup probe.syntax:
startupProbe:
  <exec | grpc | httpGet | tcpSocket>: ...
  failureThreshold: <integer>
  periodSeconds: <integer>

parameters.name: initialDelaySeconds
parameters.description: Seconds after container start before the first startup probe.

parameters.name: periodSeconds
parameters.description: Seconds between startup probe attempts. Default 10; minimum 1.

parameters.name: timeoutSeconds
parameters.description: Seconds before one probe attempt times out. Default 1; minimum 1.

parameters.name: successThreshold
parameters.description: Consecutive successes needed after failure. Must be 1 for startup probes.

parameters.name: failureThreshold
parameters.description: Consecutive failures that mark the startup check as failed. Default 3; minimum 1.

parameters.name: probe mechanism
parameters.description: One probe mechanism: exec, grpc, httpGet, or tcpSocket.

Startup probe.returns: The probe result is Success, Failure, or Unknown. A failed startup probe causes the kubelet to kill the container and apply its restart policy.

example.title: Startup probe for a slow container
example.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: slow-starting-app
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: nginx:1.27
      ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
      startupProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /healthz
          port: 8080
        failureThreshold: 30
        periodSeconds: 10
example.explanation: This gives the container up to 300 seconds for its startup check to pass.

useCases.title: Slow initialization
useCases.scenario: The application loads large files, configuration, or migrations before it can serve requests.

useCases.title: Protect liveness checks
useCases.scenario: The container needs a separate startup window while keeping a quick liveness check afterward.

useCases.title: Long startup time
useCases.scenario: The application has a long first start and should not be restarted before initialization finishes.

interview.question: What problem does a startup probe solve?
interview.answer: A startup probe protects slow-starting applications. While it has not succeeded, Kubernetes pauses liveness and readiness checks for that container. If it reaches its failure threshold, the kubelet kills the container and applies the restart policy.
interview.followUp: How would you choose its timing? Multiply failureThreshold by periodSeconds and make that window longer than the worst expected startup time, without making the liveness probe itself slow to detect deadlocks.

interview.question: When should you use a startup probe instead of a long liveness delay?
interview.answer: Use a startup probe when initialization can take longer than the normal liveness timing allows. It lets the application finish loading data, configuration, or migrations before liveness checking begins.
interview.followUp: Why not only increase liveness initialDelaySeconds? A startup probe separates the startup window from ongoing health checks, so liveness can remain responsive after startup.

interview.question: How is a startup probe different from liveness and readiness probes?
interview.answer: A startup probe runs during startup and must succeed before liveness and readiness probes begin. Liveness detects when to restart a running container, while readiness controls whether the Pod receives Service traffic.
interview.followUp: Can readiness and liveness succeed independently? Yes. They do not depend on each other, although both are delayed when a startup probe is configured.

keyPoints: It checks whether the application inside the container has started.
Liveness and readiness checks wait until the startup check passes.
The startup check is for initialization, not continuous health monitoring.
failureThreshold sets how many consecutive failures cause the startup check to fail.
gotchas: A startup probe that never succeeds causes the kubelet to kill the container; the Pod restart policy then applies.
Set failureThreshold and periodSeconds so the allowed startup time covers the slowest normal startup.
A startup probe must use successThreshold: 1; higher values are not allowed.

StatefulSet.summary: A StatefulSet manages Pods that keep stable names, network identities, and storage. It also provides ordered creation, scaling, and rolling updates for stateful workloads.
StatefulSet.explanation: A StatefulSet manages Pods that each keep a unique identity. The identity includes an ordinal number, a stable hostname and DNS name, and storage from the Pod's PersistentVolumeClaims. It creates and updates Pods in order by default, and keeps each Pod's identity when the Pod moves to another node.
StatefulSet.syntax:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: <name>
spec:
  serviceName: <headless-service>
  selector: <label-selector>
  template: <pod-template>

parameters.name: spec.replicas
parameters.description: Desired number of Pod instances. Defaults to 1 when omitted.

parameters.name: spec.serviceName
parameters.description: Service that governs the StatefulSet network identity. It must exist before the StatefulSet.

parameters.name: spec.selector
parameters.description: Label selector that must match the labels in the Pod template.

parameters.name: spec.template
parameters.description: Pod specification used to create the StatefulSet Pods.

parameters.name: spec.volumeClaimTemplates
parameters.description: Claims used to create per-Pod persistent storage.

parameters.name: spec.podManagementPolicy
parameters.description: Controls whether Pods use OrderedReady or Parallel management.

parameters.name: spec.updateStrategy
parameters.description: Controls Pod updates: RollingUpdate, OnDelete, or Recreate when its feature gate is enabled.

StatefulSet.returns: A StatefulSet resource whose status reports the current, ready, available, updated, and revision-related Pod counts.

example.title: StatefulSet with stable identity and storage
example.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  serviceName: web
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: registry.k8s.io/nginx-slim:0.24
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 80
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /data
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata:
        name: data
      spec:
        accessModes: ["ReadWriteOncePod"]
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 1Gi
example.explanation: This creates a headless Service and a StatefulSet with two Pods. Each Pod gets a stable name, such as web-0, and its own storage claim.

useCases.title: Stateful databases
useCases.scenario: A database cluster needs each member to keep its identity and data volume after rescheduling.

useCases.title: Ordered distributed systems
useCases.scenario: A distributed system starts members in order and stops them in reverse order.

useCases.title: Stable network identities
useCases.scenario: Each replica needs a stable hostname for peer discovery.

StatefulSet.since: v1.26 for the first availability of configurable start ordin

interview.question: When should you use a StatefulSet instead of a Deployment?
interview.answer: A StatefulSet is used when replicas need stable identities, stable storage, or ordered operations. Each Pod keeps an ordinal, a network identity, and storage association across rescheduling.
interview.followUp: How does a StatefulSet provide stable DNS? It uses the serviceName field with a headless Service, producing names based on the StatefulSet name and Pod ordinal.

interview.question: What ordering guarantees does a StatefulSet provide?
interview.answer: The default OrderedReady policy creates Pods from ordinal 0 upward and removes them from the highest ordinal downward. The controller waits for required readiness or termination conditions before proceeding.
interview.followUp: How can ordering be relaxed? Set podManagementPolicy to Parallel; Pods can then be created or removed together without waiting for one another.

interview.question: How does a StatefulSet rolling update work?
interview.answer: RollingUpdate replaces Pods from the largest ordinal toward the smallest. The control plane waits for the updated Pod to become Running and Ready before updating its predecessor.
interview.followUp: How can you update only higher ordinals first? Set rollingUpdate.partition; Pods with ordinals at or above that value update, while lower ordinals remain unchanged.

keyPoints: Each Pod identity has three parts: an ordinal index, a stable network identity, and stable storage.
For N replicas, the default Pod indexes are 0 through N-1.
A Pod hostname combines the StatefulSet name and ordinal, such as web-0.
The controller adds the apps.kubernetes.io/pod-index label with the Pod's ordinal.
Every volume claim template gives each StatefulSet Pod its own PersistentVolumeClaim.
gotchas: Deleting or scaling down the StatefulSet does not normally delete its storage. Remove unused volumes manually when data deletion is intended.
Create the headless Service yourself before relying on StatefulSet Pod DNS names.
Deleting the StatefulSet does not guarantee ordered Pod termination. Scale it to zero first when graceful, ordered shutdown is required.
Do not force StatefulSet Pods to have zero termination grace time. The documentation calls this unsafe.

StorageClass.summary: A StorageClass describes a type of storage that Kubernetes can dynamically provide for PersistentVolumeClaims. It names the provisioner and storage rules, such as reclaim behavior, expansion, topology, and binding timing.
StorageClass.explanation: A StorageClass describes a storage option that Kubernetes can use to create PersistentVolumes for PersistentVolumeClaims. Its provisioner, parameters, reclaim policy, expansion setting, mount options, and binding mode control how that storage is created and used.
StorageClass.syntax:
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: <name>
provisioner: <provisioner>

parameters.name: provisioner
parameters.description: Identifies the volume plugin or external provisioner used to create PersistentVolumes.

parameters.name: parameters
parameters.description: Provider-specific settings for volumes in this class.

parameters.name: reclaimPolicy
parameters.description: Policy for dynamically created PersistentVolumes: Delete or Retain.

parameters.name: allowVolumeExpansion
parameters.description: Whether PVC requests may grow the volume.

parameters.name: mountOptions
parameters.description: Mount options applied to dynamically created PersistentVolumes.

parameters.name: volumeBindingMode
parameters.description: When binding and dynamic provisioning occur: Immediate or WaitForFirstConsumer.

parameters.name: allowedTopologies
parameters.description: Node topology limits for dynamically provisioned volumes.

StorageClass.returns: A non-namespaced StorageClass object that describes dynamic PersistentVolume provisioning.

example.title: A StorageClass for delayed binding
example.code:
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: fast-storage
provisioner: csi.example.com
reclaimPolicy: Retain
allowVolumeExpansion: true
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
parameters:
  type: fast
example.explanation: This class asks an external CSI provisioner to create fast storage. It keeps the volume after release, permits growth, and waits until a Pod uses the claim before binding.

useCases.title: Define storage choices
useCases.scenario: An administrator offers storage with different speed, backup, or service policies.

useCases.title: Enable dynamic provisioning
useCases.scenario: A PVC needs storage created automatically instead of selecting a pre-created PersistentVolume.

useCases.title: Handle topology-aware storage
useCases.scenario: A volume must be created in a topology that matches the Pod's scheduled node.

useCases.title: Allow volume growth
useCases.scenario: A workload needs to increase its storage request later.

interview.question: What is a StorageClass used for?
interview.answer: A StorageClass defines a storage class and the rules for dynamically creating PersistentVolumes. A PVC can request it by name, or Kubernetes can use the default class when no class is requested.
interview.followUp: What happens if several classes are marked as default? Kubernetes uses the most recently created default when a PVC has no storageClassName.

interview.question: How do Immediate and WaitForFirstConsumer differ?
interview.answer: Immediate binds or provisions storage as soon as the PVC is created. WaitForFirstConsumer delays that work until a Pod using the PVC is scheduled, which helps account for node topology.
interview.followUp: What should a Pod use instead of nodeName with WaitForFirstConsumer? Use a node selector, because nodeName bypasses the scheduler.

interview.question: What do provisioner and parameters control?
interview.answer: The provisioner identifies the volume plugin or external program that creates the PersistentVolume. Parameters are provider-specific, so their accepted names and values depend on that provisioner.
interview.followUp: Does Kubernetes include an internal NFS provisioner? No. NFS needs an external provisioner, such as an NFS CSI driver or another compatible external provisioner.

keyPoints: Administrators use StorageClass objects to describe different storage options.
The required provisioner selects the plugin or external program that creates volumes.
Dynamic volumes inherit the class reclaim policy: Delete or Retain.
Set allowVolumeExpansion to true to permit a PVC to request more storage.
If volumeBindingMode is omitted, Kubernetes uses Immediate binding.
A PVC uses the StorageClass name to request a specific storage option.
gotchas: Omitting reclaimPolicy can delete a dynamically created PersistentVolume when it is released.
Expansion increases a volume only. It cannot reduce the requested size.
With WaitForFirstConsumer, use nodeSelector instead of nodeName so the scheduler can place the Pod.
Do not set mountOptions unless the selected provisioner supports them.

Taints and tolerations.summary: Kubernetes taints mark nodes to repel Pods. Tolerations in a PodSpec let Pods match taints, but they permit scheduling rather than guaranteeing it.
Taints and tolerations.explanation: A taint marks a node so Pods without a matching toleration are rejected or discouraged. A Pod declares tolerations in its PodSpec. Kubernetes removes tolerated taints from consideration, then applies the remaining effects: NoSchedule blocks placement, PreferNoSchedule discourages it, and NoExecute can evict a running Pod.
Taints and tolerations.syntax:
kubectl taint nodes NODE KEY[=VALUE]:EFFECT
spec:
  tolerations:
  - key: KEY
    operator: Equal|Exists
    value: VALUE
    effect: NoSchedule|PreferNoSchedule|NoExecute
    tolerationSeconds: SECONDS

parameters.name: kubectl taint nodes NODE KEY[=VALUE]:EFFECT
parameters.description: Node name and taint specification, such as key=value:NoSchedule.

parameters.name: spec.tolerations
parameters.description: Pod toleration fields include key, operator, value, effect, and optional tolerationSeconds.

example.title: Taint a node and tolerate it
example.code:
kubectl taint nodes node1 dedicated=team-a:NoSchedule

kubectl run workload --image=nginx --overrides='{"spec":{"tolerations":[{"key":"dedicated","operator":"Equal","value":"team-a","effect":"NoSchedule"}]}}'
example.explanation: The taint blocks ordinary Pods. The toleration lets this Pod pass the taint filter.

useCases.title: Dedicated nodes
useCases.scenario: Keep general workloads away from nodes reserved for one team.

useCases.title: Special hardware
useCases.scenario: Leave GPU or other special hardware available for workloads that need it.

useCases.title: Eviction
useCases.scenario: Use NoExecute to remove Pods that should not remain on a node.

useCases.title: DaemonSets
useCases.scenario: Apply tolerations to DaemonSets so node-level agents continue running under relevant node taints.

interview.question: What are taints and tolerations?
interview.answer: A taint is attached to a node and repels Pods. A toleration is attached to a Pod and allows it to ignore a matching taint. A toleration permits scheduling but does not select the node.
interview.followUp: How are several taints handled? Kubernetes ignores taints matched by tolerations, then applies the effects of the remaining taints.

interview.question: How do the taint effects differ?
interview.answer: NoSchedule prevents new Pods without a matching toleration from being scheduled. PreferNoSchedule is a soft preference, so the scheduler tries to avoid the node but may use it. NoExecute also affects Pods already running there.
interview.followUp: What happens when NoExecute is added? Untolerated running Pods are evicted, while a tolerationSeconds value can delay eviction.

interview.question: How does a toleration match a taint?
interview.answer: A toleration matches by key, effect, and operator rules. Equal requires the specified value to match; Exists matches the key without requiring a value. An empty key with Exists matches all taints.
interview.followUp: Can a Pod tolerate one effect but not another? Yes. The toleration's effect limits its match; an omitted effect matches taints with any effect.

keyPoints: Taints make nodes repel selected Pods.
Use kubectl taint to add or remove a node taint.
Put tolerations in the PodSpec.
NoSchedule blocks new matching-absent Pods, but does not evict Pods that already run there.
PreferNoSchedule tells the scheduler to avoid the node when practical, without making a hard block.
An unignored NoExecute taint evicts an existing Pod and also prevents its placement.
A nonmatching PreferNoSchedule taint lowers a node's preference rather than absolutely rejecting it.
gotchas: A toleration does not force placement on the matching node. The scheduler still checks other scheduling rules.
Setting spec.nodeName skips normal scheduler decisions, so a Pod can be bound to a tainted node.
NoExecute tolerations can include a time limit. After that time, the Pod can be evicted.

VerticalPodAutoscaler.summary: Vertical Pod Autoscaler adjusts a workload's CPU and memory requests and limits to better match actual use. It is a separately installed Kubernetes add-on that uses metrics and can apply recommendations when Pods are created, recreated, or resized.
VerticalPodAutoscaler.explanation: The VPA recommender studies current and past CPU and memory use, including peaks and OOM events, then writes target, lower-bound, and upper-bound values to the VPA status. The updater compares those values with Pod requests and either changes resources in place or evicts Pods, depending on updateMode. A mutating admission webhook applies recommendations when Pods are created or recreated.
VerticalPodAutoscaler.syntax:
apiVersion: autoscaling.k8s.io/v1
kind: VerticalPodAutoscaler
spec:
  targetRef: {apiVersion, kind, name}
  updatePolicy:
    updateMode: Off | Initial | Recreate | InPlaceOrRecreate | InPlace

parameters.name: spec.targetRef
parameters.description: API reference, kind, and name of the workload to manage.

parameters.name: spec.updatePolicy.updateMode
parameters.description: Controls when and how recommendations are applied.

parameters.name: spec.resourcePolicy.containerPolicies
parameters.description: Container-specific bounds and resource controls.

VerticalPodAutoscaler.returns: The VPA writes recommendations to status.recommendation and may update or replace target Pods according to the selected update mode.

example.title: A VPA for a Deployment
example.code:
apiVersion: autoscaling.k8s.io/v1
kind: VerticalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: my-app-vpa
spec:
  targetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: my-app
  updatePolicy:
    updateMode: Recreate
  resourcePolicy:
    containerPolicies:
    - containerName: application
      minAllowed:
        cpu: 100m
        memory: 128Mi
      maxAllowed:
        cpu: "2"
        memory: 2Gi
      controlledResources:
      - cpu
      - memory
      controlledValues: RequestsAndLimits
example.explanation: This VPA targets the my-app Deployment. It can evict Pods so replacements receive recommended CPU and memory values. The policy limits the recommendation range and selects the resources to manage.

useCases.title: Observe usage safely
useCases.scenario: You want resource recommendations without automatic changes.

useCases.title: Set initial requests
useCases.scenario: New Pods need right-sized requests at creation time.

useCases.title: Resize with recreation
useCases.scenario: A workload's resource needs change over time and replacement Pods are acceptable.

useCases.title: Prefer in-place updates
useCases.scenario: The cluster supports Pod resource resizing and disruption should be reduced.

interview.question: What is the difference between VPA and HPA?
interview.answer: A VPA adjusts the resource requests and limits of Pods, while an HPA changes the number of replicas. VPA uses a recommender, updater, and admission controller webhook.
interview.followUp: How does VPA decide new values? It analyzes current and historical CPU and memory use, peaks, variance, OOM events, and available cluster resources.

interview.question: Explain the main VPA update modes.
interview.answer: Off only records recommendations in the VPA status. Initial applies them only when Pods are created. Recreate evicts Pods when requests differ enough, and the replacement receives new values.
interview.followUp: What does InPlaceOrRecreate add? It tries an in-place resize first and evicts the Pod only when that resize cannot be completed.

interview.question: How can a resource policy constrain VPA?
interview.answer: The resourcePolicy can set minAllowed and maxAllowed limits, choose managed resource types with controlledResources, and choose whether requests, limits, or both are controlled.
interview.followUp: What happens if controlledResources is omitted? VPA manages both CPU and memory for that container.

keyPoints: Create VPA objects with the autoscaling.k8s.io/v1 API version.
The recommender calculates suitable resource values from usage data.
The updater applies changes by eviction or by an in-place resize when supported.
Read the generated target, lower-bound, and upper-bound values from status.recommendation.
Use Off to observe recommendations without automatically changing running or new Pods.
Use Initial when only newly created Pods should receive recommendations.
Use minAllowed and maxAllowed to bound recommendations for a container.
gotchas: VPA is an add-on, not a built-in Kubernetes API feature. Install it before creating VPA resources.
Do not choose Auto for new configurations. Use Recreate or InPlaceOrRecreate instead.
InPlace can leave a Pod unchanged when a resize cannot happen, such as when the node lacks capacity.
